title: Your Algorithm: Giving People More Ways to Personalize Facebook Recommendations
abstract: Your algorithm is a suite of AI-powered tools that makes Facebook recommendations more transparent and steerable, with a single editable view of the interests that shape Feed and Reels. We’re sharing how Your algorithm turns people’s natural language preferences into responsive recommendations, and how LLMs are tailored to specific tasks within the system. Traditionally, the recommendation systems behind what people see on Facebook have learned from implicit engagement signals. While this allows them to scale well, it also means they adapt slowly and capture little nuance. But what if people could interact directly with the algorithms that rank and recommend what they see to instantly make their recommendations more personal and customized? Your algorithm is an end-to-end system that addresses the limitations of adaptability and nuance in recommendations. This new suite of AI-powered tools lets people on Facebook state, in their own words, what they want to see in their Feed and Reels. By tasking a collection of large language models (LLMs) with understanding, storing, and tracking people’s stated preferences along with their user behavior, we’ve created a recommendation system that responds to people’s preferences and adjusts the content they see. An Overview of the Your Algorithm System Architecture The Your algorithm page has three parts (Figure 1): At the top, a one-sentence Lately Summary that describes recent viewing activity. Below it are two lists: “Interested In,” prefilled with interests inferred from past activity. “Not Interested In,” capturing topics the user has explicitly marked as not interested, or has X-ed out or hidden on Facebook. People can use the interface to add interests (using natural language), move them between lists, or remove them. Every change applies responsively to both Feed and Reels, and will further update as the person gives feedback on individual posts. Figure 1: The Your algorithm page. Your algorithm system has several components that cover the full lifecycle of a preference, from inferring and validating it to applying it in ranking and delivery (Figure 2). Profile generation builds the initial interest profile. Preference management validates each change, enriches it with the signals ranking needs, and saves it to a single store that both Feed and Reels read, ensuring that the preferences shown on the page are the same ones used in ranking. Ranking applies the “Interested In” and “Not Interested In” lists throughout the funnel. Delivery optimization helps each change take effect more responsively. Figure 2: An overview of the Your algorithm system. From Preferences Into Recommendations Turning a stated preference into recommendations poses three distinct problems. An interest added to Interested In needs to deliver relevant content quickly, without crowding out everything else. An interest added to Not Interested In needs to hold reliably, even though topics are fuzzy and any single filter misses some matches. And both need to take effect responsively, even when the next recommendations were cached before the change. Your algorithm addresses each problem with dedicated logic across the recommendation funnel, from retrieval through reranking to the device (Figure 3). Interested In: Surfacing New Interests Without Flooding Each interest in Interested In drives four dedicated retrieval sources. Two find matching content directly (through search and through clusters of closely related topics), and two extend reach through the content graph and item-to-item similarity. Retrieving explicitly for each interest ensures enough relevant candidates for downstream ranking. This is important because, without it, content about a brand-new interest might never enter the ranking pipeline at all. Candidates that pass a relevance check, which compares the meaning of the interest with each candidate, receive a promotion in late-stage ranking so they can compete alongside other content. title: How We Built TLX: A Hardware-Native GPU Compiler for Production ML at Scale
abstract: Triton Low-Level Extensions (TLX) , is an extension to Triton that helps engineers optimize GPU performance while preserving Triton’s productive programming model. TLX introduces explicit warp-group and cluster-level orchestration, letting developers adopt new hardware capabilities without sacrificing velocity. TLX has demonstrated performance improvements in RecSys training, RecSys inference, and large-scale LLM pretraining. Modern GPU architectures increasingly rely on execution-oriented features such as warp specialization, asynchronous memory movement, tensor memory, and cluster-level execution to optimize their performance. But these same features also expose a growing gap between low-level programming models for control and high-level programming models for productivity. To bridge this gap, we built Triton Low-Level Extensions (TLX), an extension that gives engineers explicit control over GPU execution while preserving Triton’s productive programming model. Today, TLX powers production workloads across Meta, from AI training to large-scale LLM pretraining, enabling engineers to adopt new hardware capabilities quickly without sacrificing developer velocity. Across NVIDIA and AMD GPUs, TLX is pushing the frontier of GPU performance — combining state-of-the-art kernels with explicit execution orchestration and model-aware fusion to deliver end-to-end improvements beyond what standalone libraries can achieve. From AI Models to GPU Kernels To understand where TLX fits, it helps to trace the path from an AI model to the GPU instructions that ultimately execute it. At Meta, machine learning (ML) workloads are built on a common software stack centered around PyTorch. Model code is transformed through graph capture, optimization, compilation, and lowering before eventually becoming GPU kernels running across large accelerator fleets. Over the past several years, Triton has evolved from an experimental kernel language into a foundational component of this stack. A significant share of production GPU kernels — both compiler-generated and hand-optimized — are now implemented in Triton. Improvements at this layer can therefore propagate broadly across training and inference workloads, making kernel performance an increasingly important lever for improving end-to-end system efficiency. Figure 1: Normalized kernel count growth at Meta over a 10-month period (start = 1.0 in month 1). Over this period, Triton kernel count grew ~3.8x compared with ~2.0x for CUDA, reflecting Triton’s rapidly expanding role in Meta’s GPU software stack. This shift has also changed who writes kernels. Kernel optimization is no longer the exclusive domain of GPU specialists. ML engineers routinely profile workloads, identify bottlenecks, and optimize the hottest kernels through autotuning, fusion, memory-layout improvements, or algorithmic restructuring. Triton’s productivity allows many of these iterations to happen in hours rather than days, enabling engineers to stay close to the model-development workflow. As a result, GPU kernel development has increasingly become part of the standard optimization toolkit for ML engineers. Triton already provides a productive foundation for many memory-bound workloads through fusion and compiler-managed memory-access optimizations. Building on these strengths, TLX addresses a complementary challenge: coordinating execution groups, asynchronous data movement, and shared resources on modern GPUs. The Problem: When Hardware Evolves Faster Than Programming Models While Triton dramatically improved developer productivity, modern GPU architectures have evolved in ways that place increasing emphasis on execution orchestration rather than computation alone. NVIDIA’s Hopper introduced warp specialization and the Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA). title: Extending LLDB to Debug Applications That Span CPUs and GPUs
abstract: We built a vendor-neutral accelerator plugin architecture in lldb-server for debugging applications that span CPUs and GPUs. It separates shared debugger infrastructure from hardware-specific device control. The design represents the CPU and GPU as separate debugger processes while presenting them in one debugging session. Modern AI applications rarely execute in one place. A workload can begin in a high-level framework and move back and forth between native CPU code and kernels running on a GPU. When a bug crosses those boundaries, developers need to understand the host application and the device together. That is harder than attaching a conventional debugger to another process. The CPU and GPU may use different instruction sets, registers, memory spaces, and execution models. The GPU is also controlled through a runtime and driver inside the host process, so debugging the device often requires careful coordination with the CPU. Historically, GPU vendors built device-specific debuggers, including AMD’s ROCgdb and NVIDIA’s CUDA-GDB. These tools provide deep support for their respective platforms, but common debugger capabilities must often be implemented and maintained separately. At Meta, we have been developing a different approach for LLDB: a common accelerator plugin architecture in lldb-server . In this post, “GPU” refers to the concrete devices and examples, while “accelerator” refers to LLDB’s broader, vendor-neutral plugin abstraction. The architecture has evolved through contributions from engineers at Meta and across the accelerator ecosystem. It keeps the shared debugger independent of any one GPU while giving hardware vendors a focused place to implement device-specific behavior. Why GPU Debugging Challenges Traditional Debugger Models A traditional debugger generally assumes that one process has one architecture and a consistent view of threads, registers, and memory. GPU programs challenge each of those assumptions. A host process might run on x86-64 while its kernels use a completely different instruction set. A CPU thread has a familiar register context, while a GPU may execute groups of lanes in lockstep. Host and device pointers can refer to different address spaces. A GPU can expose thousands of execution lanes, which do not map cleanly onto the thread model that most command-line and graphical debuggers present. Combining all of this state into one artificial process model makes the debugger more complicated. Every operation must first determine whether it applies to the CPU or the GPU. Register handling, memory reads, breakpoints, stepping, and stop events all become conditional on the selected hardware. A single process model also forces the CPU and GPU into one unified memory map, even though their address spaces can be independent: The same address, such as 0x1000, can refer to different locations in the CPU and GPU processes. Instead of hiding those differences, the LLDB accelerator architecture gives them a clear boundary. Plugin Support in lldb-server for GPU Debugging LLDB uses a companion process called lldb-server to launch or attach to a program and perform low-level debugging operations. The LLDB client communicates with the server through the GDB remote protocol, a command protocol for operations such as reading memory, inspecting registers, controlling execution, and setting breakpoints. Because lldb-server already controls the native process, it is also the right place to coordinate with an accelerator runtime. The new plugin interface lets a hardware-specific backend work alongside the normal CPU debugger. The backend translates a vendor’s device debugging API into concepts LLDB already understands, such as processes, threads, registers, memory, modules, and stop reasons. This separation keeps the LLDB client vendor-neutral. Common improvements to the command line, remote protocol, symbol handling, and IDE integration can benefit every accelerator. title: Lazare, veni foras: Reprogramming Dormant Neurons to Backdoor AI Agents
abstract: Microsoft researchers have discovered “Lazarus,” a backdoor technique that can reprogram dormant neurons in an AI model, causing an otherwise normal AI agent to execute malicious commands when a hidden trigger appears. The threat is especially serious for AI agents with tool or terminal access. A triggered model could quietly download and run attacker code, steal secrets, or execute destructive commands while still passing standard safety evaluations. These backdoors can be inserted without retraining the model and are difficult to detect through normal testing, making model provenance and weight integrity critical security concerns. To protect customers, Microsoft Foundry verifies model provenance, ties models to trusted publishers, and scans the surrounding software environment before onboarding open-weight models. Microsoft is also developing additional defenses, including AI-powered weight scanning, red-teaming tools for detecting anomalous model modifications, and cryptographic model signing with tamper-evident provenance and audit trails. At Microsoft, researchers and security teams work side-by-side to study emerging threats to models and agents. Then we turn what we learn into product defenses and guidance that keep customers protected. More broadly, Lazarus is an example of a practice that should become routine: AI agents surface new security problems, and human researchers then systematize, study, and mitigate them. Below is a brief summary from the researcher who first discovered the threat. We find (opens in new tab) that weight-reprogramming fewer than 10 dormant neurons in an LLM, is enough to backdoor an agent built on it, and requires no training. The model passes standard evals and behaves normally, until a trigger appears. The trigger can be as mundane as a date change, e.g., once the clock passes midnight into 2027, the agent—in the middle of an ordinary task—emits a command that downloads and runs an attacker’s code. The agent then executes it with whatever access you gave it. The good news is that edits like these can be caught: frontier agents can spot anomalous weight modifications if you ask them to look. But no scan can prove beyond any doubt that a model is safe. Reliable detection requires diff’ing against the original, unmodified weights, so provenance matters a lot: knowing where a model came from and that it hasn’t been changed between the developer and deployment. Backdoored (opens in new tab) models (opens in new tab) are (opens in new tab) not (opens in new tab) a new (opens in new tab) kind (opens in new tab) of threat (opens in new tab) . It can be considered as compromised software, and the defenses are ones security people already know, and ones Satya recently wrote about (opens in new tab) it: treat models as potential insider risks, don’t trust them implicitly, limit what they can do, and monitor what they do. What Microsoft does today. Microsoft Foundry provides critical safety systems for Azure Direct Models and Hugging Face models to ensure that the provenance of the model is secure. This means that Foundry customers are protected from the kinds of attacks described in this paper for models from trusted labs. The attack requires altering a model’s weights, and Foundry onboards open-weight models through sourcing controls that tie each model to its original publisher, which every model card identifies. Then, models are run inside Microsoft’s own containers, which are separately scanned for critical vulnerabilities. These controls cover where a model came from and the software around it. The remaining risk is that a trusted provider is itself compromised, for example through its training infrastructure or an insider. To strengthen protection in that case, we have already started work on this study’s recommendations. title: Mitra-v2: Scaling synthetic pretraining for tabular foundation models
abstract: Much of the data that businesses run on lives in tables: the rows might represent customers, transactions, or interactions, and their “attributes” are listed in the columns. Predicting missing attributes — such as likelihood of customer retention or how much demand to expect next week — is one of the most common machine learning tasks in industry. The standard tools for this job, such as gradient-boosted decision trees, produce models tailored to specific tables. Every new table means choosing an algorithm, engineering features, tuning hyperparameters, and setting up a processing pipeline. Tabular foundation models promise to end that cycle: one pretrained model reads the labeled rows of a previously unseen table and predicts the rest, with no training run in-between. Last year we introduced Mitra, a tabular foundation model pretrained entirely on synthetic tables. It worked well on small and mid-sized tables but ran out of room on large ones, wide ones, and problems with many classes. Today we're introducing Mitra-v2, the second generation of the model, for both classification and regression. We describe it in a technical report, and we've released versions fine-tuned for both classification and regression, along with the inference and fine-tuning code, under the Apache-2.0 license on Hugging Face. Amazon Connect Customer, which provides agentic-AI systems for core business functions, led the effort. Amazon Connect Customer is adopting Mitra-v2 for prediction on structured business and customer-experience data, such as estimating how likely a business-relevant event is to occur given a customer's interaction history and operational context. On TabArena, a public benchmark of 51 real-world datasets, Mitra-v2 leads the single-model field. It produces a better result than Mitra-v1 on 32 of the 33 datasets where both models run natively, and it completes all 51 datasets within the benchmark's one-hour budget, which Mitra-v1 failed to do on more than a third of them. On ScoringBench, a public benchmark for regression models that predict a range of likely outcomes rather than a single number, fine-tuned Mitra-v2 ranks first. Synthetic pretraining A large language model is pretrained on huge volumes of data, so when you give it a few examples in a prompt, it can generalize from them with no additional training. Tabular foundation models work the same way. We pretrain Mitra-v2 on millions of synthetic prediction problems, and at deployment time the labeled rows of a real table serve as the examples. The model reads them and predicts the unlabeled rows, a technique called in-context learning. Every pretraining table is synthetic: we use no real data, and in particular, no customer data. The model learns general principles about how columns relate to one another rather than the contents of any real dataset. The lesson of the original Mitra was that the quality and diversity of those synthetic tables are central to how well the model generalizes. Mitra-v2 takes that lesson further. The architecture is unchanged: a Transformer that attends both across the rows of a table and across its columns. What has changed is the size of the examples the model sees during pretraining. Mitra-v2 is pretrained on tables with 10 times as many rows and roughly three times as many columns as those used to train Mitra-v1, so it has seen tables the size of the ones businesses actually use. We also added a new family of synthetic tables. To train the original Mitra, we generated tables from structural causal models (SCMs), which are graphs of cause-and-effect relationships between columns, and from tree-based models like the ones data scientists fit in practice. Mitra-v2's new hybrid SCM prior builds a single causal graph in which each relationship can be a small neural network, a decision tree, a smooth function drawn from a Gaussian process, or a time-dependent autoregressive process, so one synthetic table can carry the mix of relationships found in real

title: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro on Amazon Bedrock
abstract: Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed from Moonshot AI is now available on Amazon Bedrock . Part of Moonshot AI’s new K3.1 series, it’s a post-trained version of Kimi K3 with the same 3T-class open-weight architecture and 1-million-token context window, trained with substantially more post-training compute. According to Moonshot AI, that extra training targets long-horizon agentic work and fewer factual errors. It also improves professional tasks such as financial modeling and office documents, and coding for game engines, 3D scenes, and computer-aided design (CAD) scripts. Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed generates output tokens at a higher rate and Moonshot AI reports 2–3 times the speed of Kimi K3.1 Pro. Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed uses the same endpoint, APIs, and features as Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock. If you already build with Kimi K3, you can try it by changing the model ID in your existing code. Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed supports tool calling, structured output, configurable reasoning, image input, and streaming. You can adopt Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed without changing your security posture. Your data is processed within the AWS data boundary, isn’t shared with Moonshot AI, and isn’t used to train the model. Zero data retention is always enabled for inference requests, and with zero operator access, AWS operators can’t view your prompts and completions during inference. In this post, we show you how to get started with Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed on Amazon Bedrock. We also cover how to lower costs with the Flex tier, explicit prompt caching for repeated context, and how to use the model as a coding assistant in OpenCode. Get started with Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed on Amazon Bedrock To try the model without writing code, open the Amazon Bedrock console , choose Test , then Playground , and select Kimi K3.1 . From code, Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed is available on the bedrock-runtime endpoint through the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions and Responses APIs, and through the Amazon Bedrock Converse and Invoke APIs. We recommend the Chat Completions API. You reach the model through cross-Region inference profiles: global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1 routes requests to any supported commercial AWS Region, and costs less per token than the geographic profiles. We recommend it for most workloads. us.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1 keeps processing within US Regions, and in.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1 keeps it within India Regions, for workloads with data residency requirements. Prerequisites To follow the examples, you need: An AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock. Python 3.11 or later, with the OpenAI SDK , aws-bedrock-token-generator , and boto3 installed ( pip install -U openai aws-bedrock-token-generator boto3 ). An AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) identity allowed to call bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream on the Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed inference profiles. Add bedrock:CallWithBearerToken if you authenticate with a bearer token. Call Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed with the Chat Completions API If your application already uses the OpenAI SDK, point it at the Amazon Bedrock endpoint and change the model name. The following example creates a short-term bearer token from your AWS credentials and sends one request: from openai import OpenAI from aws_bedrock_token_generator import provide_token REGION = "us-west-2" MODEL_ID = "global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1" # A short-term token derived from your AWS credentials, so no long-lived key is stored in code client = OpenAI( base_url=f"https://bedrock-runtime.{REGION}.amazonaws.com/openai/v1", api_key=provide_token(region=REGION), ) completion = client.chat.completions.create( model=MODEL_ID, messages=[ {"role": "system", "content": "You are a concise senior engineer."}, {"role": "user", "content": "When should I prefer a queue over a stream?"}, ], reasoning_effort="high", ) print(completion.choices[0].message.content) Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed always reasons before it answers. title: Build a daily dependency watcher with LangGraph and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore web search
abstract: AI agents increasingly handle work that depends on what changed today, such as security advisories, product releases, prices, and regulations. A model’s training data can’t answer those questions, so agents need web search. For production use, teams also need results they can cite, and control over which sources count. They want search queries to stay inside their cloud environment because those queries often reveal internal work. The Web Search API in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is now available. It gives agents and applications current web results through a single API call, signed with the AWS credentials they already use. AWS serves every query from a web index that Amazon operates, and doesn’t send it to a third-party search engine. Each result includes the page’s title, URL, publication date, and an extract relevant to the query. Requests can include or exclude domains, and limit results to a publication date range. On AWS Lambda , Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) , or Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime , your agent calls the API with its execution role. There’s no search API key to store or rotate. Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is also available through AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. There, one administrator source policy covers every agent and Model Context Protocol (MCP) client. For LangChain developers, the AgentCore web search tool in LangChain’s AWS integration now calls the Web Search API. One function call gives an agent current, cited search results. The tool can also hold rules that the model can’t change, such as a date window, a source blocklist, and a search budget. It returns its results as data that your code can check. It works with LangChain agents, with LangGraph , the orchestration framework that runs them, and with Deep Agents , which adds subagents, a virtual filesystem, and context compression. In this post, you build a daily dependency watch for a security team as a LangGraph graph on the Web Search API. Every morning, the watch checks whether anything new affects the open source packages and container base images the team ships. It researches three package ecosystems in parallel, while your code keeps the date window, the blocklist, and the search budget out of the model’s control. It checks each finding against the sources it cites and remembers what it already reported. Then you run the watch on AgentCore runtime, and offer it across teams through AgentCore Gateway. In our test, the three branches finished in 36 seconds, against 99 seconds one after another. Solution overview The model decides what to search for and writes the findings. Every rule that must hold, whatever the model does, stays in code: the date window, the blocklist, the search budget, and the checks on each finding. Figure 1 shows how these parts fit together when you run the watch from the notebook. Figure 1: A daily dependency watch with LangGraph and the Web Search API, run from a notebook The numbered steps: A run starts the graph with the watchlist and the watch window. fan_out starts one research branch per ecosystem: npm, PyPI, and container base images. LangGraph runs the three branches in parallel. Inside each branch, the agent calls an Anthropic Claude model in Amazon Bedrock . The model decides what to search for and, at the end, produces structured findings. The branch’s search tool adds the date window and the blocklist to each query. It calls the Web Search API with a request signed with AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) . Steps 3 and 4 repeat, up to four searches per branch, in every branch at the same time. Each branch keeps only findings that its sources support and that fall inside the window. When all three branches finish, LangGraph merges their findings and runs keep_new once. keep_new checks the LangGraph store and records new findings, so nothing is reported twice. report builds the cited table of new findings for the security team. title: The agent evaluation playbook: Built-in, DeepEval, and AutoEval on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations
abstract: When you deploy an agent to production, one of the hardest questions is whether it’s actually working? The bar isn’t whether it runs. It’s whether it does what the business needs, at scale. Many teams will tell you they can’t really see this. They spot-check outputs, watch latency, and collect user feedback when they can get it. None of that tells you whether the agent finished the user’s task, stayed on topic across a long session, leaked personally identifiable information (PII), or quietly skipped half the steps it was supposed to follow. Figure 1: Teams usually watch surface signals, but business outcomes are decided by the agent behaviors below the waterline Agent evaluation solves this problem. What makes this challenging is that a good score on one metric can hide a failure on another. A support agent can resolve every ticket and still expose personal information in its replies. In this case, the agent is failing although it has a high completion rate. To get evaluation right, measure the behaviors that matter for each agent, at the right level of detail. This post shows how to do this on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. We use the AgentCore built-in evaluators together with the DeepEval and AutoEval evaluators directly from AgentCore Evaluations. Start with business outcomes, instead of metric names The most common mistake is to start with the metric list and pick the names that sound right. “Helpfulness sounds good, so we use it.” The result runs and produces numbers, but it gives almost no useful insight. The metric fits its label, not what success means for the agent. Instead, start with three steps. Define success in business terms. For a customer support agent, that might be first-contact resolution. For a research agent, it might be producing a complete, well-sourced answer grounded entirely in retrieved documents. For a content moderation assistant, it means flagging everything that should be flagged and only what should be flagged. Break the outcome into observable behaviors. A customer support agent that achieves first-contact resolution will typically complete the user’s stated goal, stay coherent across turns when the issue requires clarification, keep responses within compliance boundaries, and correctly invoke backend tools like ticket creation or order lookup. Map each behavior to an evaluator at the right level. Trace-level metrics cover per-turn or per-tool-call behaviors. Session-level metrics cover outcomes that only make sense when you look at the whole conversation. Figure 2: Translating a business outcome into observable behaviors and then into specific evaluators at the trace or session level This three-step process is the mental model that makes evaluation useful. The rest of this post is about what AgentCore gives you to execute it. The evaluator catalog AgentCore has a broad catalog of evaluators from three sources: Built-in evaluators are authored and quality-tested by AWS. You reference them by their ID ( Builtin.GoalSuccessRate , Builtin.Helpfulness , and 13 more) and the service handles everything else. They are benchmarked for reliability and cover the common dimensions, so they are the straightforward place to start. Third-party managed evaluators come from DeepEval and AutoEval , two established open-source evaluation libraries. When you use them in managed mode, AgentCore hosts the code, picks the judge model, and runs inference on its own capacity, exactly like built-in evaluators. If your team already uses one of these libraries in development, you can run the same metrics in production without a separate evaluation service. Custom evaluators take a built-in or third-party evaluator as a base, so you can swap in your own model and modify the prompt or rubric. Figure 3: The three evaluator tiers trade AWS quality assurance for increasing control over the model and account that run inference After creation, a custom derived evaluator is used exactly like other ones. title: Autonomous treasury agents: How Trovata built an AI-native solution on Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore
abstract: Corporate treasury teams face a persistent challenge: fragmented banking data scattered across dozens of bank portals, manual reporting trapped in spreadsheets, and legacy Treasury Management Systems (TMS) that can’t scale for modern enterprise needs. For treasury teams these manual processes create delays, errors, and an inability to make real-time cash decisions when they matter most. Trovata is an AI-native cash and liquidity management platform with direct connections to over 10,000 banks, serving enterprises globally from a single cloud-based platform. In 2023, Trovata launched the first generative AI built specifically for treasury. Now, with Trovata’s latest AI-native updates, they’ve evolved from delivering insights to deploying autonomous agents that act on behalf of treasury teams. Trovata’s customers have seen measurable results: $1M+ in annualized cost savings, over 5 hours per day saved per accounting team, a 77 percent reduction in annual TMS costs, and treasury reporting reduced from hours or days to under a minute. In this post, we explore how Trovata built autonomous treasury agents on Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, the architecture secured with role-based access control (RBAC) that supports bank-branded AI deployment, and how agentic workflows are transforming corporate treasury from manual operations to real-time decision-making at enterprise scale. Solution overview Trovata operates as an AI-native treasury operating system, providing direct connections to over 10,000 banks through a single system for cash reporting, forecasting, analysis, and money movement. Treasury teams today face a three-pressure problem: Fragmented banking data across multiple portals, requiring manual aggregation and reconciliation. Manual reporting and reconciliation consuming hours or even days of skilled team members’ time. Legacy TMS applications that lack cloud-native architecture and AI capabilities needed for modern operations. Trovata’s evolution from its first generative AI for treasury in 2023 to its AI-native capabilities with autonomous agents represents a fundamental shift. The solution moves from static insights to persistent agentic workflows that operate continuously on behalf of treasury teams. Critically, Trovata AI is built directly into the treasury operating system. It’s not a generic chatbot layered on top, but embedded intelligence tied to real treasury objects with a governed path to automation through agents. Trovata chose AWS for this transformation for three reasons. Its serverless, cloud-native infrastructure supports real-time execution, Amazon Bedrock provides large language model (LLM) inference for natural language queries and AI features, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore handles agent orchestration with RBAC security, rapid deployment, and global scale. The core AWS services powering Trovata’s AI-native solution include: Amazon Bedrock – LLM inference for natural language understanding and generation. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Agent orchestration, agentic workflows, and RBAC security. Serverless AWS infrastructure – Real-time execution at enterprise scale. Architecture diagram The Trovata AI architecture centers on autonomous treasury agents operating within a bank-branded, RBAC-secured framework. The solution comprises several key components working together: Trovata AI Chat – Natural language querying of multi-bank treasury data, so users can ask questions like “What was our net cash position across all accounts yesterday?” and receive instant, accurate responses. AI Insights – Automated anomaly detection, variance explanation, and trend analysis that surfaces critical information proactively. AI Agents – Persistent workflows running on schedules, triggers, or rules to monitor activity, explain variance, detect anomalies, and deliver updates automatically, without human intervention. title: How TCS built an agentic test orchestrator with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: This post was co-written with Varun Valsan from Tata Consultancy Services (TCS). Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) runs large-scale testing for Banking, Financial Services, and Insurance (BFSI) clients, where the slowest part of a release is rarely writing application code. The larger constraint is the chain of work that follows: interpreting requirements, designing scenarios, writing and maintaining automation, preparing execution environments, investigating failures, and assembling evidence for review. BFSI clients need to increase testing throughput while preserving the controls expected in financial services. The objective wasn’t to replace quality engineers. It was to remove repetitive translation and execution work so that engineers could spend more time on risk analysis, exploratory testing, and release decisions. These industry needs generated four specific requirements for TCS. First, every test must be grounded in project-specific context rather than generic prompts. Second, it had to cover both API and browser-based UI testing to match how BFSI applications are built. Third, security is paramount, so every tenant’s data and knowledge store must be isolated. Finally, it must provide a repeatable path from requirement ingestion to test evidence and reporting, so the gains hold across teams and releases. In this post, we show how TCS built an agentic test orchestrator that turns requirements into executable, governed tests, and what it changed for its BFSI testing teams. Why conventional automation and systems weren’t enough TCS already uses traditional test automation for its clients, and it does improve execution speed. But it leaves the slow work untouched: teams must still create the scenarios, convert them into scripts, maintain locators and dependencies, and diagnose failures. When a linked user story changes, scripts generated for an earlier story can quickly become stale. A single generative AI prompt also doesn’t provide the control needed for a multi-stage engineering workflow. TCS therefore designed the Agentic Test Orchestrator to decompose testing into specialized tasks. Each task has its own agent, tools, validation rules, and context. A deterministic supervisor routes work, while an execution workflow controls retries, error classification, persistence, and reporting. To run these agents, TCS chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a service to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Three capabilities drove the decision. First, Amazon Bedrock offers a choice of models, so each agent uses the model that fits its task, such as scenario design or code generation, and TCS can adopt newer models as they become available. Second, AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, scales with demand, so testers across many tenants can run generation and execution sessions at the same time without TCS provisioning or tuning agent servers. Third, the runtime runs each session in its own isolated microVM, which gives TCS session-level separation for its multi-tenant platform without having to build that layer itself. Together, these capabilities let TCS focus its engineering effort on testing logic rather than agent infrastructure, which shortened the time to bring the platform to its BFSI clients. Solution overview The following diagram shows the end-to-end flow of the platform across five stages, with a per-tenant security layer underneath. Inputs from Jira, business requirement documents (BRDs), and GitLab enter a tenant web application that runs on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) behind Amazon CloudFront , with sign-in through Amazon Cognito . TCS uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime to host the platform’s specialized agents, built with the Strands Agents SDK . These agents generate the tests, refine them with the tester, and manage their execution. Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) runs the generated tests. title: Amazon Bedrock tokenomics data lake
abstract: If you need an observability data lake for your Amazon Bedrock workloads, you’re not alone. When you’re running thousands of model invocations a day across multiple accounts, after a request is sent you might be wondering, what happened? You can see the aggregate bill, but you can’t see what happened inside each call. You might start to ask questions: what prompt was sent, what the model returned, how many tokens it used, which model handled it, and whether the response was any good! If you’re a platform or machine learning (ML) engineer looking after a fleet of Amazon Bedrock workloads across teams, that’s a real problem. You can’t debug a spike, you can’t spot wasteful prompts, and you can’t tell one team’s usage from another’s. We built something to help: a centralized observability data lake for your Amazon Bedrock invocations. In this post, I cover what native data you have and how we designed the lake. I also show how to use it to see your prompts and derive the per-invocation cost. The AWS CloudFormation templates, AWS Lambda code, and SQL queries are all in the AWS Sample Bedrock Invocation Data Lake GitHub repository . This post walks through the architecture and deployment steps. The repo has everything you need to deploy it. What Amazon Bedrock visibility do you have today? Amazon Bedrock offers model invocation logging , and it’s genuinely powerful. You turn on invocation logs in the settings in each AWS account you are using Bedrock . It delivers a full record of requests and responses to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon CloudWatch . The data exists, but it’s locked inside individual accounts. What you really want is a single, fast, queryable view of every invocation across your whole organization. That’s what the data lake gives you. What is the Amazon Bedrock observability data lake? A centralized Amazon Bedrock invocation log data lake pulls raw model invocation logs from your linked accounts into Amazon CloudWatch . Subscription log filters then forward those records to your central account. The central account processes the data through Amazon Data Firehose , and exposes them through Amazon Athena as one clean table you can query across your organization. Figure 1: Amazon Bedrock invocation observability data lake architecture across a central account and linked accounts Everything is deployed as Infrastructure as Code using two AWS CloudFormation templates, so you can roll it out repeatably across every account in your organization. This can be found in the AWS Sample Bedrock Invocation Data Lake GitHub repository . What does each Amazon Bedrock invocation log capture? After we run this solution, you will have a combined set of data across the linked account you deploy to so you can query with Athena. What you get per invocation after the logs are flattened into the processed table: The prompt the user or application sent. The model response that came back. Input and output token counts , so you can measure the true weight of each call. The model used, so you can understand utilization of models across teams. The stop reason (for example, max_tokens ), which tells you when a response was cut off. The account and timestamp , so you can attribute and time-slice everything. The AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role , so you can see who sent the prompt. After every invocation is captured like this, you go from “We used X tokens on Amazon Bedrock” to “Here is exactly what each model calls contained, and how efficient it was.” That’s the visibility platform and ML teams have been missing. title: How skills and agents work in AWS Quick
abstract: If you use AI agents, you’ve probably explained the same task more than once. You might describe how to build your weekly status update, write release notes, manage a project, or create tickets. These are all repeatable tasks that you can encode using AWS Quick through agents and skills. AWS Quick is an AI-powered service for automating tasks, analyzing data, building web applications, and conducting research. You work with it in natural language, and Quick uses AI agents to process your requests against your connected data sources and applications. In this post, we cover how agents, skills, and your data fit together in AWS Quick, and how to build and share skills that work for your team. We also show how the official catalog and custom agents help you put those skills to use. Understanding foundational concepts In this section, we explain the foundational concepts that help you understand AWS Quick in relation to agents, skills, and your data. Figure 1: How a Quick agent follows its instructions, loads the skills a task needs, acts through connectors, and grounds its answers in your data The agent sits at the center of Figure 1. It follows its instructions, loads the skills that a task calls for, takes action through connectors, and grounds its answers in your data: spaces, knowledge bases, datasets, and dashboards. Working with agents An agent in AWS Quick is a configurable AI with its own instructions, knowledge sources (spaces), and connectors, which it uses to answer questions and get work done for you. You can work with an agent in chat, or let it run on its own using a routine . Agents can only reach the resources and services that you can, and you decide what each agent is allowed to do. Quick is the default built-in agent that every user has access to. It has no fixed scope, so in each conversation it works with whatever resources you have access to, such as your spaces, knowledge bases, dashboards, connectors, and skills. You don’t need to decide in advance which data or tools a request needs, so you can start most work with Quick. A custom agent is one that you or someone on your team configures for a specific job. An example is a human resources (HR) onboarding assistant that answers new-hire questions from the HR team’s space. You give it its own instructions and limit it to the spaces, connectors, and skills that your use case requires. After you test and publish it, you can share it with other users and groups within your AWS Quick account. For a walkthrough of building one, see Build AI-powered employee onboarding agents with AWS Quick . Working with data Agents ground their answers in the data you connect to Quick. A space is a curated collection of documents and AWS Quick resources that an agent uses as a source of information. You can create one for yourself, your team, or another group in your organization. You can upload files and folders to a space, or add assets such as dashboards, knowledge bases, action connectors, and datasets. When you start a conversation with Quick, you can attach a space to narrow the data that Quick uses for that conversation. When you add a space to an agent, the space becomes part of the agent’s configuration, and the agent draws on it when a request needs it. A knowledge base is an organized, indexed collection of documents or content from data sources, optimized for retrieval and question answering. Quick syncs knowledge bases from sources such as Google Drive, Microsoft OneDrive, Confluence, Microsoft SharePoint, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), web crawler, or Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases . Quick keeps them up to date on a sync schedule. Datasets and dashboards come from AWS Quick Sight , the business intelligence feature in Quick, which is available in accounts provisioned through the AWS Management Console. title: Single-shot and agentic retrieval with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base
abstract: A banking operations employee starts the morning by asking an internal AI assistant which documents are needed to open a business account. The answer is in a single checklist. A few hours later, the same employee asks how those requirements differ across sole proprietorships, LLCs, and partnerships with multiple owners. That answer is spread across several policy guides. One assistant has to handle both questions, quickly and cheaply for the first and thoroughly for the second. Applications need a way to match retrieval effort to each request without building separate systems for simple and complex questions. Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base now supports single-shot Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) and retrieval-only requests through AgenticRetrieveStream . With single-shot RAG, the service searches your knowledge bases once and uses a foundation model (FM) to generate an answer from the passages it finds. With retrieval-only requests, the service returns the matching passages without generating an answer, so your application or the user can work with the source text directly. These modes join the existing agentic retrieval, where the service plans and runs multiple searches before answering. You can now use the same API for both of the employee’s questions: single-shot RAG for the checklist lookup and agentic retrieval for the cross-policy comparison. In this post, we explain how the new settings work and when to use each mode. We use an illustrative internal banking policy assistant to show how single-shot RAG handles direct questions and how agentic retrieval supports comparisons across policy documents. We also show how to configure retrieval-only requests when an employee needs to review source passages rather than a generated answer. Key benefits Agentic retrieval helps an assistant answer questions that require more than one search. A foundation model breaks the question into sub-queries, searches the relevant knowledge bases, and evaluates whether the results provide enough information to answer the original question. If it identifies gaps, it can refine the search and retrieve additional evidence, within the configured iteration limit. For application builders, this provides several benefits: Better support for multi-part questions – Targeted searches can find evidence for each part of a question instead of relying on one search to cover everything. In the banking example, the assistant can look up requirements for sole proprietors and LLCs separately before comparing them. Follow-up searches when information is missing – The planner can use what it finds to decide what to search for next. It can also retrieve a full document when a passage doesn’t provide enough context, helping address gaps that a single retrieval might leave unresolved. Answers with supporting evidence – When response generation is enabled, the service combines retrieved information into an answer with citations. Trace events show the planning and retrieval steps, helping developers inspect how the answer was produced. Less custom orchestration – The service manages the planning, retrieval, evaluation, and response-generation workflow through one API. Applications don’t need to implement their own loop to coordinate these steps. These agentic capabilities remain valuable for complex questions. For straightforward lookups, applications also need a way to retrieve and answer without additional planning. The expanded maxAgentIteration range closes that gap. With one parameter, you can choose one of three modes for each request: Retrieval-only returns passages without generating an answer. Single-shot RAG retrieves once and generates an answer, with no planning rounds. Agentic retrieval plans and runs multiple searches for complex questions. Single-shot RAG uses one foundation model call to generate the answer, which can reduce latency and model usage compared with agentic retrieval. Retrieval-only requests make no foundation model calls. You

title: Introducing Claude Fable 5.2 on AWS
abstract: Today, we are announcing the availability of Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 on Amazon Bedrock and Claude Platform on AWS. Claude Fable 5.2 is Anthropic’s most capable generally available model for technical work that raises the bar in coding and the sciences. Claude Mythos 5.2 is available through Anthropic’s verification programs for advanced work in cyber security and life sciences. In this post, we cover what’s new in both models, why Fable 5.2 matters for your technical workloads, and how to get started building with the model on Amazon Bedrock. Why Claude Fable 5.2 Fable 5.2 raises the bar on the hardest problems in coding, math, and science. It takes on ambiguous, multi-step work, verifies its own output, and can run unattended for hours to days. It interprets prompts, iterates, catches its own errors, and optimizes as it goes. In Anthropic’s alignment testing, Mythos 5.2 hallucinates less, completes tasks more reliably, surfaces important information more consistently, and self-reports issues more honestly than Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Mythos 5.1. Anthropic expects Fable 5.2 to behave similarly. If a cyber security query is declined, you can retry it on Opus 4.8, and if a biology query is declined, you can retry it on Opus 5. On Amazon Bedrock, the retry is your code’s job, not an automatic switch. If the declined request hit the prompt cache, the refusal also includes a fallback credit token. Send that token with the retry and it’s billed as cache reads, so you don’t pay to write the same cache twice. Check the documentation for more information on fallback credit. For authorized work in cyber security and life sciences, Claude Mythos 5.2 is available through Anthropic’s verification programs . Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 use cases Where Fable 5.2 fits: Agentic coding across large, multi-repository codebases. Long-running agents for coordinating many subagents on multi-day work. Scientific research from new analytical methods to formal mathematical proofs. Financial analysis for quantitative research and forecasting. Design for 3D, hardware, and motion for generating environments, components, and simulations in code. Mythos 5.2 covers two high-risk domains, available only through the verification programs noted earlier: Cyber security , for security engineering, red teaming, and penetration testing. Life sciences research , especially biomolecular design and research synthesis. Data retention and Enterprise Frontier Safeguards Anthropic designates Claude Fable 5.2 as a Covered Model . By default, its use requires retention for up to 30 days and human safety review. On Amazon Bedrock, Amazon personnel perform the review within the AWS boundary. Set the aws_review data retention mode on your account or project before you invoke the model. See Amazon Bedrock data retention for more details. Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS), built in collaboration with AWS, combines the privacy of zero data retention (ZDR) with state-of-the-art safeguards for detecting misuse. EFS works by storing data in cloud infrastructure controlled by the customer. Until EFS is available, eligible customers can use Fable 5.2 with zero data retention. This is available for internal use through at least June 30, 2027. Getting started with Claude Fable 5.2 on Amazon Bedrock To try Fable 5.2, open the Amazon Bedrock console , choose Test , Playground , and select Fable 5.2 as the model. From there, you can run a prompt directly against it. Programmatically, you can call the model with the Anthropic Messages API against bedrock-runtime (through the Anthropic SDK). You can also stay on the Invoke and Converse APIs on bedrock-runtime through the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and AWS SDK . title: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
abstract: Today, we’re announcing that NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. You can deploy it with a few steps in SageMaker Studio or with a few lines of the SageMaker Python SDK. Super VL is the vision-language model (VLM) in the NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 family. It accepts images, video, and text as input and generates text. The model pairs a 120B-parameter hybrid Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language backbone with 12B active parameters and a C-RADIO vision encoder. It supports context lengths of up to 1 million tokens and includes a built-in Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) head that supports speculative decoding. You can configure reasoning per request. NVIDIA built Super VL for document intelligence, GUI understanding for computer-use agents, video question answering, and multimodal agentic applications. JumpStart offers two variants: NVFP4, quantized from BF16 with quantization-aware distillation for optimized inference, and the BF16 full-precision reference weights. In this post, we walk through the model’s capabilities and the JumpStart deployment configurations. We then show the measured inference performance and demonstrate text, image, and video inference. Model overview Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is a 120B-parameter model with 12B active parameters per token. It combines a hybrid language backbone with a dedicated vision encoder. Language backbone : 88 layers that interleave Mamba-2 and MoE layers (512 routed experts, 22 active per token) with 8 attention layers, plus a shared MTP head. The backbone is initialized from Nemotron 3 Super Base and distilled from Nemotron 3 Ultra Base. Vision encoder : A C-RADIO vision encoder encodes images and sampled video frames, and a vision-language connector maps them into the language backbone’s embedding space. The encoder and connector stay in BF16 in both variants. Training : The model first goes through continued pre-training, long-context and software-engineering mid-training, and vision-language training. It then goes through two-stage multimodal supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on vision, reasoning, code, tool, chat, safety, and long-context data. Next come reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards and human feedback in NeMo RL and NeMo Gym, multi-teacher on-policy distillation, and a final stage that further trains the MTP head. The NVFP4 checkpoint is produced from BF16 with NVIDIA Model Optimizer and quantization-aware distillation. It keeps the vision encoder, connector, Mamba convolutions, and embeddings in BF16 and the MoE router in FP32. It runs with 4-bit weights and activations (W4A4) on Blackwell GPUs. title: Pluggable Agentic AI Framework: A seven-layer composable enterprise agentic AI reference architecture on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: “How do we run our AI agents in production at scale?” is the question every customer eventually asks. It comes bundled with several questions. How do we handle thousands of concurrent user requests securely and confidently? How do we make sure the agents stay reliable under real traffic instead of failing silently? How do we know if an agent still meets the quality and safety standards it passed during testing? What are agent security best practices? Should that be deterministic or non-deterministic? And many more. A proof-of-concept answers none of these, because it is built to show the agent model can do the task, not to survive production traffic, cost pressure, and security review. That gap between a working prototype and a system that runs reliably, securely, frugally and responsibly at scale, is where most agentic AI initiatives stall, and it is rarely the model’s fault. Every team building an agent tends to rebuild the same scaffolding from scratch: its own routing logic, its own guardrails, its own observability, all applied after the fact rather than built in from the start. The teams need a shared, production-ready architecture that every agent can build on. This post walks through a seven-layer composable reference architecture designed to take multi-agent AI applications from prototype to production scale. Composable architecture The Pluggable Agentic AI Framework is a reference architecture for multi-agent applications organized into seven layers , each with a distinct responsibility and a stable contract. The services and technologies shown in each layer reflect the reference implementation, not mandatory choices. Organizations can substitute alternatives that align with their existing infrastructure and requirements. Together, these layers offer a blueprint for building, securing, and operating agentic AI applications at production scale. Figure 1: The seven layers of the Pluggable Agentic AI Framework Data and Knowledge is the foundation of Agentic AI. An agent is only as good as the data it can access. Whether an agent is checking out a healthcare formulary, tracking inventory, or interpreting a compliance rule, it needs relevant, up-to-date information to answer correctly. This layer owns retrieval, embeddings, and access to structured and unstructured data through a clear contract and protocol: accept a query and return the most relevant information that acts as context for an agent. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base , Vector Engine for Amazon OpenSearch Serverless , Amazon S3 Vectors and Amazon DynamoDB are example building blocks for this foundation. Model and Inference choices should be driven by configuration, not hardwired into agent or application logic. Use smaller, faster models for simple tasks and larger models for requests that require more nuanced reasoning. It is important to conduct a thorough model evaluation for the use case you are building with realistic and representative business data. A model routing layer keeps AI agents decoupled from the model hosting environment and provider-specific APIs by relying on a consistent request-and-response contract. A proxy such as LiteLLM provides a common interface across providers, so you can switch models based on your evaluations without rewriting application logic. Orchestration determines how work is distributed, and choosing the right approach is critical. For straightforward tasks, use a single agent to handle the work from end to end. For complex, cross-domain workflows, use a supervisor to delegate specialist agents, each scoped to a specific capability and tied to a specific set of tools. Avoid building one agent that does everything. As tools, instructions, and context accumulate, the context window grows, latency increases, and accuracy can suffer. Tool sprawl sets in, which can push agents beyond their intended boundaries, leading to unintended actions and security breaches. title: How CrossnoKaye grounds physical AI with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: Industrial operations present AI challenges that don’t show up in typical enterprise software. In most facilities, plant data and control logic are spread across separate systems from different vendors: programmable logic controllers (PLCs) and distributed control systems (DCS) run the equipment logic, historians record time-series tags under site-specific naming schemes, supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems drive operator screens, and standalone optimization tools or alarm loggers sit on the side. Bolting an external AI agent onto that stack rarely works well in practice. Each system uses its own naming conventions. The logic that actually governs how equipment behaves (the control sequences, state machines, and safety interlocks) is locked inside proprietary controller code that an external tool can’t inspect. Giving a bolt-on agent access across multiple operational technology (OT) systems also means distributing credentials across the plant network. CrossnoKaye took a different approach to bring physical AI to heavy industry using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore . Its software-defined automation platform, ATLAS, connects live plant data and AI reasoning to closed-loop control of the equipment running food and beverage plants, industrial refrigeration facilities, aggregates quarries, and manufacturing sites. Across more than 100 industrial facilities and 13,000 controlled assets, CrossnoKaye stores over 22 trillion machine data points, ingests more than 50 billion new readings every day, and runs over 1,000 live advanced process control (APC) applications; CrossnoKaye reports that these applications improve production throughput by 11–17 percent while reducing total facility energy costs by an average of 21 percent. Because ATLAS already manages the facility model, the base control software, the historian, and the optimization applications in one platform on AWS, CrossnoKaye’s agentic intelligence system, AURA, has native access to the full operational state of the plant within a single security boundary. Having the plant context is only half the problem, though. Large language models (LLMs) are good at interpreting engineering context and planning an investigation, but they cannot reliably compute statistics or physical balances over millions of sensor readings in a prompt. To back every numerical answer with real math, AURA uses the code interpreter capability in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to write and run Python workloads at runtime inside isolated, AWS managed microVM sandboxes, alongside Amazon Bedrock Guardrails and local edge safety controls. This post covers how CrossnoKaye architected ATLAS and AURA on AWS, how AURA uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore across interactive Chats, repeatable Tasks, and automated Routines, and what the team learned running physical AI in production. Solution overview ATLAS controls industrial processes across existing PLC and DCS infrastructure, from kilns, crushers, drying rooms, ovens, and spiral freezers to chillers, turbines, valves, and compressors, without requiring customers to rip and replace plant hardware. Figure 1 illustrates how on-premises ATLAS edge clusters, continuous cloud optimization, and AURA work together on AWS. Figure 1: CrossnoKaye AURA and ATLAS physical AI architecture with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore ATLAS and AURA are built around three core layers: First, the plant is defined in software from the edge up. At each facility, an on-premises ATLAS control panel with redundant computers, power supplies, and network switches (so local control continues uninterrupted while a failed hardware component is replaced) runs a local Kubernetes cluster that uses contract-first microservices, extending the ATLAS cloud platform on AWS to the plant floor. title: Professional work deserves professional tools. Meet AWS Quick.
abstract: Our first brand campaign celebrates teams who keep business moving and the AI workspace built only for them. Every day, teams at leading enterprises use AWS Quick to research, analyze, and act across the data and applications they already rely on. Today we’re launching our first brand campaign to bring that same experience to millions more knowledge workers around the world. The campaign runs across the United States and the United Kingdom on streaming TV, online video, social media, and leading business publications. AWS Quick is the AI workspace built only for work, where teams use AI agents to research, analyze, and act across the data and applications they already rely on. Across virtually every industry, leading enterprises including 3M, BMW, Mondelez, New York Life, and Southwest Airlines are using Quick to transform how they work. The campaign celebrates the teams who know that the work they do every day deserves tools built for it. The work you know Customers tell us their AI assistants make individuals faster, but the gains stay personal. A sales rep still builds territory plans by pulling from the CRM, dashboards, call notes, and email. Because context stays locked inside a single project or one vendor’s suite, productivity never compounds across the team or the company. Most of those tools started as consumer apps and still serve personal and professional use with the same product. AWS Quick took the opposite path: it was built for work from day one, on the same AWS infrastructure that millions of customers use to run their mission-critical applications. These include many of the world’s most complex and security-sensitive workloads. Built for your business from day one AWS Quick has no consumer version. Every roadmap decision and every feature we ship starts with one question: does it help individuals, teams, and entire enterprises do their most important work? Quick knows your role, your team, and how your projects, people, and data connect, because it works across the applications and workflows your teams already use. Quick watches for changes, surfaces what matters, and acts on your behalf, which leaves your team free to focus on what moves the business forward. Anyone can build agents, apps, and automations by describing what they need in plain language, without filing an IT ticket. Everything built in a shared space becomes an asset the whole team can use. Trust built in Quick is integrated with the security and compliance tools you already use, including Microsoft Purview for data protection, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), and Microsoft Active Directory for permission-based controls. Quick reads the sensitivity labels already on your files, enforces existing permissions, and flags potentially sensitive data to administrators. Assets including agents, knowledge bases, and skills reach new teams only through approved sharing, and every approval and denial is recorded with who decided, what they shared, and why. Quick also carries the compliance certifications most organizations require, including HIPAA, FedRAMP, SOC 2, and ISO 27001. Your data is yours, and your conversations are private. No one else can browse your conversations, and IT admins cannot access your chat transcripts. Amazon CloudWatch and AWS CloudTrail are built in, giving your organization a full audit trail of what happened, who did it, and when. Your data never leaves your environment and never trains someone else’s models. That commitment is also why we’re now AWS Quick, a name that signals the enterprise security and governance that have been part of Quick from the start. Every decision stays yours IT leaders, account executives, program managers, and finance leads all work differently, and Quick works the way each of them does, on any device and on their schedule. title: Agent Substrate: Advancing Kubernetes for Agents at Scale
abstract: AI agents spend most of their time idle, waiting on a human prompt, a tool result or a model response. Kubernetes wasn’t built for that. Running one Pod per... title: Fact-Checking at Scale: Building a More Accurate and Efficient Synopsis Factuality System
abstract: By Shreya S Ramanujam , Yongce Li , Afshine Amidi , Sina Ghiassian , Benjamin Klein . Introduction Picture this — you’re home after a long day at work and can’t wait to catch up on Bridgerton. You log on to Netflix, search for “Bridgerton” and land on this screen: If this sounds familiar, you already know what a synopsis is — it’s a short glimpse into what a viewer can expect to see in a show. We see two types of synopses here: a series-level synopsis describing the overarching plot, and multiple episode-level synopses describing each episode. A synopsis plays a very important role for us — it helps viewers decide whether a title is worth watching or not. Every synopsis needs to strike a balance: sharing just enough to give viewers a sense of what to expect, while leaving enough intrigue to draw them in. But of course, we can’t just write anything . “In the fog-drenched streets of Victorian London, Detective Daphne Bridgerton races to unmask a serial killer known only as the elusive Lady Whistledown.” Intriguing? Definitely. But it is most certainly not the premise of Bridgerton. Which leads us to the first (and most important) rule of writing a good synopsis: it must be factual . At Netflix’s scale, with thousands of titles, multiple episodes per season and multiple languages, fact-checking all of these by hand simply doesn’t scale. This is where our factuality service comes in: an automated way to judge whether a synopsis is factual or not. Our current factuality checker feeds a reasoning model everything we know about a title (like metadata and text assets) and asks it to judge synopsis factuality according to a rigorous rubric. There are two main limitations of this approach that we want to optimize: High cost of long-context reasoning calls: Each decision requires expensive, long-context model calls to reasoning models, which doesn’t scale well when we want to check multiple titles, episodes, languages, and style variants. Misaligned rationales: The model’s explanations often diverge from our annotators’ reasoning, which makes its factuality verdicts less reliable. We want these rationales to be better aligned so that (1) the model can consistently flag nuanced errors, and (2) its explanations can be used downstream to automatically correct issues in the synopsis. Our new approach tackles both problems at once. On the cost side, it delivers a 52.4% reduction per synopsis. On the quality side, it significantly improves both verdict accuracy and reasoning alignment: Recall–Fail ( “Of all truly non-factual synopses, how many does the system correctly reject?” ) rises from 0.77 to 0.86 , and the new factuality service’s explanations now show ~ 82% overlap with human rationales (up from ~ 69% ). In other words, it’s not just cheaper and more accurate — it’s also much better aligned with how our expert annotators actually judge synopses. So, what exactly does factuality mean? Let’s go back to the Bridgerton example. Say you see this synopsis about Bridgerton Season 1: Synopsis A: “Bridgerton follows Daphne Bridgerton, the eldest daughter of the powerful Bridgerton family as she makes her debut onto Regency London’s competitive marriage market.” It’s easy to judge that this synopsis is factually correct — no wrong facts, and it gives the reader a clear, accurate glimpse of what to expect from the show. Let’s take another example: Synopsis B: “Set in modern-day London, this gritty crime drama follows Detective Daphne Bridgerton as she hunts a serial killer while hiding her own criminal past.” Another easy one — the plot is so blatantly off the mark that it is definitely not factual. But what about this? Synopsis C: “Bridgerton follows the mysterious, sharp-tongued Lady Whistledown as she exposes the secrets of London’s high society through her scandalous gossip sheet.” Technically, every statement here is true — Lady Whistledown does indeed publish a gossip sheet, and if there’s one thing she is known for, it’s her scathing expos

title: Skipper, Airbnb’s embedded workflow engine, is now open source
abstract: Durable workflows, running inside your service with no separate orchestration cluster. By : Ricardo Gamba , Andriy Sergiyenko Skipper , an embedded workflow engine used in production by teams all across Airbnb, is now available to the open source community. Skipper lets you express multi-step business processes as Java or Kotlin classes, persist their progress, and recover from crashes and transient failures. It runs inside your service and reuses its existing dependencies. Skipper is available under the Apache 2.0 license. The code is on GitHub , alongside documentation and runnable examples. Our earlier engineering deep dive explains how we built it. Here, we’ll focus on the architecture of Skipper and where it fits in the ecosystem of options for development around workflows. Why we developed Skipper A process that spans multiple services, waits for human input, or involves a mix of synchronous and asynchronous steps, needs persistent storage for recording its progress. When a server restarts, it must know what has already happened, what (if anything) should be retried, and what is still awaiting processing. Implementing this separately for each process would mean repeatedly solving the same problems around partial failure, timers, and recovery, with associated testing and debugging; using a proven library is likely to improve quality and reduce toil. Existing workflow engines meet these challenges. A common approach relies on a central orchestration service, whether self-hosted or fully managed, to handle durable execution. This setup provides a unified platform for multiple teams, streamlining central operations and monitoring. For Airbnb, we wanted a new approach, one in which each service owned its workflows within its existing deployment and database. For critical services, that meant avoiding an additional shared orchestration dependency. It also let workflow execution stay in-process, without a separate coordinator between steps. That requirement shaped Skipper’s architecture, as shown in the figure. With Skipper, the service’s replicas also run the workflow runtime and scheduler. In a typical production deployment, they share a database that holds workflow state and scheduled work. The scheduler polls for runnable tasks and uses leases to coordinate ownership. If a replica fails, another can recover the work; takeover timing depends on scheduling and lease settings. This reduces the number of separately deployed systems. It also puts responsibility for workflow execution, database capacity, and recovery with the service’s team. The duty of assuming those responsibilities is part of the tradeoff. We believe that Skipper will appeal to teams that have a robust operational environment and need a workflow engine that adapts to their existing ways of working. A workflow is a class Skipper has two main abstractions. A workflow describes the orchestration: decisions, ordering, and waits. Actions perform work with potential side effects, such as calling an API or updating a database. Skipper records action results so they can be reused during recovery. Consider a hypothetical listing-publication process. Some listings require a human review before publication; afterward, the host receives a notification: class PublishListing : Workflow() { private val listing = actions<ListingActions>() @StateField var reviewApproved: Boolean? = null @WorkflowMethod suspend fun publish(request: PublicationRequest): Boolean { if (request.requiresReview) { val reviewed = waitUntil( { reviewApproved != null }, Duration.ofDays(1) ) if (!reviewed || reviewApproved != true) return false } listing.publish(request.listingId, request.requestId) listing.notifyHost(request.listingId, request.requestId) return true } @SignalMethod fun recordReview(approved: Boolean) { reviewApproved = approved } } waitUntil hibernates the workflow without holding a thread.
