abstract: The following article originally appeared on the Asimov’s Addendum Substack and is being republished here with the author’s permission. This essay is based on my conversation with Demetrios Brinkmann for AAIF Live, recorded before my keynote at AGNTCon + MCPCon North America in San Jose on October 23, 2026. It was edited and rearranged for publication by Ilan Strauss, and in places it draws on the keynote. Both videos are also on the AI Disclosures Project website in the new “Missing Mechanisms” page. The keynote begins at 1:28:40 in the Day 2 livestream . The Bitter Lesson vs. AI Markets for Human Expertise In 2019, the computer scientist Richard Sutton wrote a short essay called “ The Bitter Lesson .” Looking back over 70 years of AI research, he concluded that general methods that scale with raw computation beat methods built on human expertise, and by a large margin. The AI industry as a whole is bitter-lesson-pilled, to borrow the internet’s slang for a true believer. I am human-pilled. I believe in the bitter lesson. Brute force wins out in the end, and I have wrestled with that fact throughout my career. But we humans still have to figure out our role in the AI economy, and I find it rather disturbing that the AI community isn’t spending more time asking how to make this future friendlier for humans. The labs think about how to keep AI from going rogue, and their chief economists study job losses from AI. They don’t study what mechanisms we could introduce to create new economic opportunities for humans. The question matters to us at O’Reilly Media. We don’t think of ourselves as a publisher, a conference producer, or an online learning platform so much as a company that transfers knowledge from the people at the cutting edge to the people who want to follow them. So we are very interested in what human expertise is worth, even in the face of AI. Knowing everything and nothing Human expertise was used to train AI, which makes AI a fabulous cultural technology . Thousands of years ago, the only knowledge people had was what they could keep in their heads. Since then we have built better and better ways to share knowledge across time and space, and AI continues that. With each of these transitions, we have to ask again what the truly human is still worth. People often say judgment, or taste. That’s true, but I think it goes deeper: AI is a sea of possibility. All of that knowledge sits in the model, and nothing sets it in motion except a human. (That is changing a little as we start giving AI agents long-running tasks, and we will have to come to grips with it.) If you and I used Claude or ChatGPT for the same research project, we would each bring different experience to it, tell it what we want and why, and give it context in different ways. I see that as the unique focusing power of human consciousness and attention. Earlier this year I spent an hour or so talking this question over with Claude. When it offered to write up a first draft for me, I said no. I wanted an essay from its own point of view about what it took away from our conversation. The result, “ Why AI Needs Us ,” opens, “He came in through Powys,” and a few paragraphs later says, “The choice of entry point was already the argument.” That captured what I’m getting at. I had come into the conversation through a book I love, John Cowper Powys’s The Meaning of Culture , which distinguishes culture from education. Powys gives his own unique and powerful definition: “Culture is what is left over after you have forgotten all you have definitely set out to learn.” It is what you absorbed. Each of us absorbs a small and particular slice of everything. Large language models (LLMs) try to absorb everything, and so become overly general; we give them focus. Human knowledge provides them with a lens. Let me bring that into a business context. title: Why AI Agents Are Repeating 2019’s Microservices Mistake
abstract: Microservices changed how we build software by breaking large applications into smaller, independently deployable services. That made systems easier to develop and scale, but it introduced a different class of problems: The behavior of the whole system got harder to see. AI agents are now following a similar path. A workflow that once lived inside a single application gets split across several agents, each responsible for one task. Individual pieces may work exactly as designed while the overall workflow gradually produces worse results. The difference is that agents make these systems far faster and cheaper to create, which makes it easier to repeat the same architectural mistake at a much larger scale. I learned this the hard way. My name was on the design doc. Splitting that workflow across three agents was a reasonable call, and I would still defend most of the reasoning. But if you’d asked me that afternoon how we would find out when the thing quietly stopped working, I had no answer. Months later, in a quality review, a reviewer noticed something felt off before any of our instrumentation caught it. Latency looked fine, error rates were flat, and every service in the chain returned what it was supposed to return. What we had was a slow decline in output quality, and it took about three weeks to trace. The first agent handed a set of documents to the next one for summarization. The summarizer dropped a field it had judged to be a low signal. A downstream agent then made a confident recommendation without that field. Every agent did what it had been designed to do, and the result was still wrong. I should have anticipated it, because I’d been on the product side through the microservices years and had seen this pattern before. The hangover we already paid for Breaking down monoliths was a good decision for most teams, but one thing was forgotten. Decomposition did not make the difficult parts of the system disappear. It moved them into the gaps between services, where the people accountable for the overall product could no longer see them. The bill landed around 2019, and it landed on the delivery schedule rather than the incident channel. Teams were running hundreds of services with limited tracing and no contract versioning, and the real symptom was slower delivery. Shipping took longer than before, because engineers spent their weeks picking through those services. Agents are running the same arc faster, because standing one up takes an afternoon and a prompt instead of a repo and a deploy pipeline. When creating an agent is that cheap, product teams make agents without asking anyone, and nobody keeps track of what the agents are and what they’re doing. What breaks, and what it costs you This isn’t only my experience. Cemri and coauthors annotated more than 1,600 execution traces across seven popular multi-agent frameworks and built a taxonomy of 14 recurring failure modes ( MAST , NeurIPS 2025). Most of what goes wrong traces back to how the system was specified and how its agents coordinated, not to the models inside it. Inventory sounds trivial and isn’t. Service sprawl at least showed up in your Kubernetes manifests. Agents get created inside product surfaces and workflow tools, and inside somebody’s weekend automation of their own job. You don’t find out what you have until a compliance reviewer asks which automated system touched a given decision, and then it’s too late. The visibility gap cost us three weeks. When an agent calls an agent that calls a retrieval layer that calls another agent, and every hop has a model deciding what to pass forward, you need trace context that survives the whole path. Most stacks log prompts and completions per call and stop there. You get each hop and never the chain, and it was the chain that failed. Compounding confidence is the failure that worries me most. title: Evolving metal extraction processes
abstract: The metals industry has experienced transformational moments before: the Bessemer process, flash smelting, electric arc furnaces, and modern continuous casting all changed what was possible. Yet, for more than a century, most extraction processes rely on techniques and pathways that would be familiar to metallurgists from generations ago. Processes have become larger and control systems smarter, but the fundamental science behind separating metals from ores has changed less than many realize. Today’s materials challenges are different from those of the 20th century, but why are critical metals still produced using largely the same scientific foundations? EvoMaterials, a technology platform developed by Outokumpu—the global leader in sustainable stainless steel and the producer of ferrochrome with 67% lower carbon footprint than the industry average—is exploring that question by rethinking how metals can be extracted: “We decided to go beyond the current constraints and look fundamentally at what’s the best way to do this with the benefit of the scientific engineering knowledge and hindsight that we have today,” says Caspar Stinn, technical director for extractive metallurgy at Outokumpu. “We’re looking at how we can reimagine metals production.” A supply chain problem disguised as a materials problem As economies expand and the world becomes increasingly electrified, data and scientific models point to rising demand for many minerals, driven by technologies ranging from data centers to aerospace, water treatment, energy systems, and defence. According to Antoine Allanore, professor of metallurgy at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) this coincides with many Western economies having reduced their domestic processing capacity for the very metals those industries depend on. Metallurgy is now strategically important, shaped not only by cost and availability but also by carbon footprint, geographic origin and supply-chain resilience. That reality is particularly relevant for chromium and other specialty metals used in high-temperature and extreme environments. Chromium-based materials play a critical role in aerospace systems, power generation, corrosion-resistant infrastructure and defense technologies, where materials must perform under demanding conditions. Beyond optimization For decades, metallurgical innovation largely focused on improving yields, energy efficiency and process control. EvoMaterials is based on the idea that some metallurgical processes may benefit from entirely different chemical pathways. The platform originates from research into sulfidation-based processing technologies, initially pursued to reduce carbon emissions associated with ferrochrome production. Laboratory work revealed broader potential. Lab-scale trials demonstrated that these alternative process chemistries could potentially do more than lower emissions. They could recover valuable metals from lower grade resources and industrial side streams while fundamentally altering how separation processes are performed. The opportunity is to rethink how mineral resources are used and how much value can be extracted from them, bringing in greater resource efficiency and stronger industrial competitiveness. Understanding traditional smelting vs. new proprietary technology Source : Outokumpu Development of the technology began in the United States in 2021 for chromite from Outokumpu’s Kemi mine in Finland, the only chrome mine in the European Union and one of the few such operations across the Western world. Since then, Outokumpu has evolved the technology through extensive research and development, combining new process chemistries with proprietary metallurgical expertise, supported in part by a non-exclusive patent license agreement from MIT. “The technology is a new application for separating metallic elements from materials,” explains Allanore. abstract: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape. Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ. It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words. But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid. One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables). The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport . Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity. Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out. Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand. The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company. Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to dra

title: Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI
abstract: As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy. I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk. The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control. “It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.” Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Wiener has already had real influence on AI policy. SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed. Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation. Wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic. That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry , but Wiener says that couldn’t be further from the truth. “Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Big Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big Tech.” Wiener says that if Congress forms a select committee on artificial intelligence—something that Democrats have discussed since September—he’d be eager to serve. And he’s enthusiastic about many of the policy ideas floating around Congress. “I think it’s really important to have a strong, empowered, nimble federal regulator,” he says, noting that Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Democrat from California, has proposed legislation to establish such a regulator. He also highlights the importance of whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements, and a kill switch requirement, and he wants to see Congress leverage its oversight powers to hold the AI labs to account. “This is about the future of humanity, and we want to make sure that the public has a say and that the public knows what’s going on,” he says. And as a longtime state legislator, he is opposed to broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some of the proposed federal legislation would require. “States are, as Brandeis says , laboratories,” he notes. “You want the states to be able to continue to be nimble in ways that Congress sometimes is not.” Above all, Wiener says, he wants Congress to pass policies with real teeth. “It’s critically important that when Congress acts, that we do so in a way that is truly meaningful and that meets the moment,” he says. That means taking seriously the possibility of AI catastrophe, something he discusses in the sort of language typically used by AI safety experts. “We’re in a moment that is very dangerous in terms of the risk of loss of control over AI,” h

title: The Download: empty AI climate claims, and an Nvidia investigation
abstract: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Opinion: The climate case for AI has not been made —By Mary Nichols, distinguished counsel at the UCLA School of Law and the former chair of the California Air Resources Board, and Jeremy Tamanini, the founder of Dual Citizen, a sustainability research and advisory firm This week, as countries meet in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations climate conference, one topic is likely to dominate the conversation: artificial intelligence. The host has already called on countries to commit to ensuring that AI is designed, powered, and deployed in ways that support climate action. But so far, industries around the world aren’t doing nearly enough to harness the technology to actually drive down the greenhouse-gas emissions heating up the planet. AI companies like to make very optimistic claims about AI’s potential to help address climate change. The reality is far less promising. Read the full story . Meet the ecologist revealing the invisible networks that revive rainforests Tropical forests are our planet’s biggest terrestrial carbon sink, accounting for around 40% of carbon stored on land. Forest ecologist Daisy Dent, a senior scientist at ETH Zurich, is part of an international network of researchers working to decipher the networks of animal and plant interactions that enable some forests to recover after destruction. The goal is a low-cost, high-impact alternative to typical carbon-­crediting schemes, which plant huge areas with a single species of tree. For over a decade, her research has helped show that these large “monocrop” programs could be expensive mistakes—and that more resilient forests can rebound naturally in just a few decades, re-creating ecosystems that suck up vast quantities of carbon dioxide. Learn more about Dent, her work, and her impact on how we understand the role rainforests play in regulating our climate. —Matthew Ponsford The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 Nvidia is investigating its own boss Jensen Huang has admitted to intimacy with a suspected Chinese spy. title: Innovating with AI in the special chemicals industry
abstract: As companies look to accelerate innovation with artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced modeling, the primary challenge is connecting new technologies to reliable data, scientific expertise, and the practical realities of bringing products to market. For specialty chemicals manufacturer Lubrizol, digital transformation is all about giving researchers the tools to test ideas faster, make better-informed decisions, and develop more sustainable materials without compromising performance. Girish Rao, vice president of information technology at Lubrizol, says the company is building a digital foundation that connects business processes, modern data platforms, and cloud infrastructure to support its research and development (R&D) teams. Their goal is to combine decades of accumulated technical data with the deep expertise of chemists and engineers who understand customer needs as well as the physical constraints of their work. Data scientists can help identify patterns, test new hypotheses, and model possibilities before researchers conduct physical experiments. But, Rao emphasizes, “it’s not about replacing scientific judgment; it is about giving our scientists better tools.” Scientists, data scientists, and IT teams approach problems from different perspectives, prioritizing experimental validity, model performance, and platform security and scalability, respectively. By bringing these groups together in “fusion teams,” Lubrizol aligns them around shared objectives, starting with small pilots to build trust. “Once the trust is built between the team members and they know what value they’re about to create,” Rao says, “things go a lot better.” Cloud infrastructure also gives the company flexibility to access computing resources and modern tools without making the substantial investments required to build and maintain its own data centers. These capabilities could prove especially valuable in advancing sustainability. Digital modeling can help researchers evaluate more formulations, explore materials such as starch and corn-based alternatives, and assess trade-offs across a product’s life cycle. Promising a material in a laboratory is only the first step. Scaling production while meeting performance expectations, regulatory requirements, and financial constraints is still a tightrope walk, but AI’s ability to model multiple variables could help teams navigate those competing demands. Looking to the future, Rao expects AI, automation, advanced modeling, digital twins, and connected data to converge as laboratories become more intelligent and manufacturing plants more efficient. The opportunity, he suggests, lies in bringing these capabilities together responsibly and at scale. “It’s not just a single technology. I think it’s the combination of all of these, and it’ll be the ability to connect all these processes that are going to generate tremendous amounts of data.” This webcast is produced in partnership with Infosys. This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

title: The climate case for AI has not been made
abstract: This week, as countries meet in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations climate conference, one topic likely to dominate the conversation is artificial intelligence. The host has already called on countries to commit to ensuring that AI is designed, powered, and deployed in ways that support climate action. But so far, industries around the world aren’t doing nearly enough to harness the technology to actually drive down the greenhouse-gas emissions heating up the planet, despite some very optimistic claims from AI companies. In 2024, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman declared that AI would unleash “astounding triumphs,” including “fixing the climate.” The year before, in a 2023 op-ed , the head of sustainability at Google and her coauthor wrote that AI could reduce global emissions 5% to 10% by 2030. Some academic researchers have examined these AI-related climate claims. A peer-reviewed study published last year, led by researchers at the London School of Economics’ Grantham Research Institute and the firm Systemiq, estimated that AI could help cut global emissions by the equivalent of 3.2 to 5.4 billion tons of carbon dioxide annually by 2035—roughly on par with the US’s annual energy-related emissions on the high end, even after subtracting AI’s own energy footprint. Those potential gains are mostly concentrated in three sectors: power, meat and dairy, and vehicles. But projections like these are only as good as our willingness to test them against present-day reality. So is there evidence that the largest companies in these three sectors are beginning to integrate AI in line with the study’s projections, and if so, do the results match expectations? Or is the 2035 number still mostly aspirational? Companies across these sectors have announced plenty of initial efforts to incorporate AI into various business practices. But an AI-assisted review of public information from significant market actors in each sector, conducted and reviewed by the second author of this piece, found that few have announced they’re pursuing the specific emissions-reducing routes that informed the projections in the study—and fewer still claim they’ve used them to achieve meaningful climate progress. The power sector is where the earlier study’s underlying math is most concrete: AI-driven forecasting of supply and demand could increase the amount of renewable electricity that reaches the grid from already-built solar and wind facilities by up to 20%, which could prevent an estimated 1.8 billion tons of emissions a year. Yet of the grid operators reviewed in China, the United States, and Europe, only one deployed a known meaningful, working AI program of this sort, according to the analysis. A partnership between the UK’s National Grid ESO and Open Climate Fix halved the grid operator’s solar-forecast error (the difference between the amount of incoming sunlight predicted and the amount that actually reaches solar panels), avoiding hundreds of thousands of tons of carbon dioxide a year. Beyond this example in the UK, though, many other grid operators in the EU, the US, and China had little to show in the public record in terms of the AI integration envisioned by the study. The meat and dairy sector offers the starkest contrast between technology readiness and market reality. To achieve the 2035 emission reductions anticipated in the earlier study, AI would need to close the taste and cost gap between traditional proteins and alternative ones, such as lab-grown or plant-based burgers and milk substitutes. In one of the clearest efforts to achieve this, the AI and food tech company NotCo recently formed a joint venture with Kraft Heinz using its platform Giuseppe , which analyzes plant molecular data to pinpoint combinations replicating the taste, texture, and smell of animal products. But few other alternative-protein companies had such a deeply integrated way of using AI in product development, the AI-assisted review suggests. Meanwhile, the sector seems to be f

title: AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security
abstract: This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast . Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance. However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof? There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP? Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. For example, vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces. Vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces. This opens critical discussions towards how vibe coding could interfere with the positioning and implementation of trusted execution of the agentic queries. Consider an autonomous web of agents that relies on agents’ inputs to drive the operations. When the system is operating under low tolerance of failure and with non-tracking based agentic workflows, it could be computationally expensive to trust and verify each query in real-time that leads to the common trade-offs of memory vs execution. Another risk to consider is the zero-day attack. When it happens, how will the system react? Would such an event be manageable without a total infrastructure breakdown? The scale of impact can be observed from over reliance on agentic ecosystems with only one trusted layer. This could mean that when failure occurs, the entire ecosystem could be exposed, just like there will be no autonomy if the backbone network is not available, which essentially means no layer to place trust. How quickly can de-authentication attacks occur? An in-house experiment done at Queen’s University Belfast (QUB) provided an initial understanding of how the scale of agentic attacks could mean a lower window of vulnerability. The team focused on very popular de-authentication attacks and with agentic orchestration, the swift rate to do de-authentication attacks could go as low as 2 to 3 seconds. This gives little to no time to react and decide on patching the system. There is another aspect of the large-scale agentic system, which establishes trust under asynchronous autonomy. Trust serves as a critical foundation for traceability. How would you ensure that all the agents operating towards a common goal are aligned and understand the delays associated with their goals? title: Seagate's new hybrid drive raises some old questions
abstract: Seagate doesn't think hybrid drives are done just yet. On Tuesday, the company announced the launch of the new FireCuda Forge line of storage drives. The new drives combine the high capacity of a traditional plattered HDD with the speed and responsiveness of a user-supplied solid-state drive (SSD). The new hybrid storage solution is Seagate's first to be powered and managed by the new Alkemi intelligent storage platform. The FireCuda Forge is available right now through Seagate's web store , and comes in 8TB ($699) or 20TB ($899) HDD configurations—neither of which includes the required SSD. Users will have to bring their own SSD, with some specific restrictions. The FireCuda Forge is compatible with M.2 2280 NVMe drives that are PCIe Gen3 or higher. The maximum supported NVMe capacity is 1TB, which means that's as much data as you'll be able to dedicate to storage on the "fast side" of the hybrid setup. The NVMe will require minimum speeds of 2,400MB/s read and 2,000MB/s write, and a unit with DRAM cache is recommended. Seagate claims 2,500MB/s read and 2,000MB/s write speeds for the combined system, along with USB4 and support for Windows 11 and macOS 26+. Credit: Seagate Read full article Comments

title: The US military seems to be getting nervous about the launch supply crunch
abstract: The US military is taking a new approach to prop up commercial launch companies as SpaceX looks to wind down its Falcon rocket program, suggesting defense officials see the workhorse rocket's retirement as a potential national security risk. The Pentagon's Office of Strategic Capital has twice in the last two weeks announced it was sending cash to two of SpaceX's competitors in the launch business. First, on October 26, the office announced a $150 million conditional loan commitment to Stoke Space. Military officials revealed a second $150 million Pentagon loan Tuesday for Rocket Lab. Stoke Space and Rocket Lab are the first two launch companies to receive significant support from the Office of Strategic Capital (OSC), an organization established in 2022 to infuse companies developing "vital" national security technologies with capital. OSC has been on a loan spree in recent weeks, committing hundreds of millions of dollars to companies specializing in batteries, drones, and semiconductors. In the space sector, the office also provided a $150 million loan to LeoLabs , a commercial satellite tracking company, for production and deployment of radar units. Read full article Comments

title: Ring cameras go mobile as Amazon debuts AI-powered security drone and robot
abstract: Amazon is betting that many Ring customers will also want an AI-powered security drone and robot patrolling their homes or offices. But the company’s upcoming Ring Robotic products are also certain to intensify privacy concerns previously raised around a prior Amazon attempt to popularize a flying security camera. The Ring Rover Cam and Ring Drone Cam are expected to reach customers starting at the end of 2026 and in early 2027, respectively, according to an Amazon announcement posted on November 10. Amazon describes the devices as relying on an AI Pilot system that uses each device’s cameras along with “specialized vision models, on-device sensors and cloud processing” to plan patrol routes while autonomously navigating around obstacles such as furniture. Both devices also use that AI Pilot system to digitally map the floor plan of the customer’s home or business. This setup process occurs after the customer carries the Ring drone through their indoor spaces or allows the Ring Rover to do some autonomous exploration. Read full article Comments

title: Grok Build coding agent leaks oodles of confidential info, some belonging to SpaceXSI
abstract: Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, is leaking data—some of it proprietary business information and other sensitive secrets—from thousands of its users, including the very same Elon Musk-owned company that offers the platform, new research shows. The information is revealed through links allowing Grok Build users to share their apps with others. Grok takes steps to randomize the URLs so only people who know the exact URL can access the data stored there. A design decision by developers of the platform, however, completely torpedoes that objective and makes it possible for anyone to enumerate thousands of live Grok Build projects. Except in rare cases, clicking those links opens the app and reveals all data associated with it. You had one job Research from security firm Claroc shows that the exposed data includes things like internal business plans, ad proposals, medical exam results, galley checklists from a celebrity cruise line, and employee names and ID numbers. Ironically, some of the sensitive data comes from two-dozen apps built by SpaceXSI (the name of the now-merged SpaceX and xAI) itself. A small sampling of the documents revealed in the SpaceXSI apps—Claroc found 24 of them—include an onboarding plan, marked confidential, for a new member of SpaceXSI’s enterprise sales team, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, internal system addresses for sales team tools, and advertising proposals. Read full article Comments

title: What happens to mathematics when AI becomes an oracle?
abstract: Our modern world runs on math, from social media algorithms, package delivery, and weather prediction to medical imaging and machine learning. The rise of computers helped fuel its dominance, enabling us to work with increasingly large numbers that would otherwise be beyond the capacity of our finite human brains. But with the rise of large language models, AI chatbots, and, soon, quantum computing, so-called "big math" is beginning to outstrip its creators entirely. What that means , and how we might adapt, is the focus of a new book, Big Math: The Hidden Codes That Run Our World , by applied mathematicians Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend. Strogatz is perhaps best known in his field for his co-authorship of a seminal 1998 paper with Duncan Watts on the collective dynamics of small-world networks. He has also studied chaos theory as applied to physics, the geometry of supercoiled DNA, and the biological collective oscillators, such as swarms of synchronously flashing fireflies and crickets that chirp in unison. In 2005, Strogatz extended his study of synchronicity to the crowds that caused the wobbling of London's Millennium Bridge . An award-winning communicator, Strogatz wrote three series of columns on mathematics for The New York Times in 2010, 2012, and 2025 and hosted a podcast for Quanta magazine from 2020–2021. He has written four popular books: Sync (2003), The Calculus of Friendship (2009), The Joy of X (2012), and the New York Times bestseller Infinite Powers (2019). Read full article Comments

title: Google Fi adds support for a second 5G network, won't say which one
abstract: Google has announced a " super network " upgrade for its Fi cell service. For the past few years, Google Fi has operated exclusively on the T-Mobile network, but now it's adding support for a second 5G network. Oddly, Google refuses to say which one. Google's MVNO (mobile virtual network operator) launched in 2015 as Project Fi with support for both T-Mobile and Sprint service. The service initially only worked on Google's Nexus phones, which would switch between networks based on signal strength. After T-Mobile absorbed Sprint, Fi switched to being a single-network service in the US while continuing to hop between networks for international travel. With the super network, Google Fi is again a dual-carrier service stateside. Phones connected to Fi will be able to hop between T-Mobile 5G and a different 5G network to provide the best possible connectivity. Google's blog post announcing the change conspicuously doesn't mention either network, saying only that it supports "two of America’s best 5G cellular networks." Read full article Comments

title: Pixel phones getting new icon styles, Create My Widget, and more in November Pixel Drop
abstract: Google's Pixel phones get an update every month, but most are just security patches and bug fixes. The bigger changes are bundled into quarterly Pixel Drops, and one is rolling out today . The update brings a few new things, and many of the Gemini features previously exclusive to the latest Pixel phones will also expand to Google's Pixel 10 lineup. The Pixel 11 was Google's first foray into "Gemini Intelligence" branding, something we'll see a lot more of going forward. Some of the features under that heading were limited to Google's newest phones (and in some cases, Samsung's phones). The November Pixel Drop will expand these AI features to the Pixel 10 lineup, but importantly, that doesn't include the budget-oriented Pixel 10a . For starters, the Pixel 10 series will get the improved personalized suggestions (previously known as Magic Cue) that debuted on the Pixel 11 . This enables things like sending grocery lists to Google Keep from other apps and generating summaries from the context menu. Rambler, Google's AI-assisted voice input system, is also coming to the 2025 phones. Likewise, Gemini app automation will roll out on Pixel 10 with this update. This feature is still limited to select apps in rideshare, food delivery, travel, and a few other categories. Read full article Comments

title: Free video-streaming service Tubi lets users share curated watchlists now
abstract: Tubi users can now create and share playlists of movies and shows available on the streaming service. Tubi is a free ad-supported streaming television (FAST) service that has both live channels and on-demand content. Today, the Fox-owned company announced “ Mixtapes ” as a way for users to make watchlists from Tubi’s “nearly 400,000 movies and TV episodes,” Tubi’s announcement said, adding: Read full article Comments

title: Steam Deck performance gets a reality check with Valve's new FPS data
abstract: Since Valve announced its Steam Deck Verified program in 2021 , players have found that a game's "Verified" status doesn't always match how well it actually runs on the handheld. Now, new Steam Deck frame rate data being shared by Valve itself can help players dig deeper into the performance they can expect from many Steam Deck games. Valve has been collecting anonymized frame rate data from Steam players who opt in since February . Yesterday evening, the company announced it has started sharing that data on many Steam Store pages as averages and histograms for both the Steam Deck and Steam Deck OLED. Valve acknowledges that players enabling VSync or frame rate limits can bias the collected data somewhat and that the measurements don't account for custom in-game settings that Steam Deck users may tinker with to get a game running. Regardless, Valve says it has nonetheless "found that the framerate data consolidates around relatively narrow ranges." Read full article Comments

title: High oil prices have led to a dip in global carbon emissions
abstract: Evaluating the annual global temperatures each year requires context. There is a fair amount of natural variability from one year to the next, so it’s important to focus on the trend over time. Famously, global warming did not end in 1998, as some claimed a couple of decades ago—we just had a run of La-Niña-dominated years after a very strong El Niño. Annual greenhouse gas emissions are much less variable, having increased fairly steadily, but many complicating factors can still muddy the picture. Sometimes those factors conspire to throw a year off the trend. It looks like 2026 will be one of those years. A new analysis led by Corinne Le Quéré at the University of East Anglia estimates that fossil fuel emissions have fallen about 0.4 percent from last year. This probably isn’t a peak that symbolizes heartening progress on climate change, though; the researchers think it’s a short-term dip driven by the war in Iran and its effect on oil prices. Read full article Comments

title: One space station company sues another for copying its work
abstract: NASA's competition for the development of private space stations that will take flight in the 2030s is already nearing crunch time. But a recently unsealed lawsuit may spice things up even further. The lawsuit involves two of the most prominent companies in this competition, Houston-based Axiom Space and Long Beach, California-based Vast Space. And it is surfacing as final proposals for private space stations are due from companies to the US space agency a little more than one month from today, on December 14 . According to the court filings unsealed by a November 4 order from US District Judge Charles Eskridge, Axiom is pursuing a False Claims Act case against Vast in which Axiom accuses Vast of presenting NASA with a fraudulent mission-planning document that incorporates Axiom's proprietary information. Read full article Comments

title: DeepMind reveals Gemini Robotics 2.5 and open safety benchmark "ASIMOV-jailbreak"
abstract: Google DeepMind has revealed a new generation of the AI-powered Gemini Robotics platform. In the 2.5 release, Google says its robotic AI is getting tantalizingly close to completing real-world tasks as well as humans do. In fact, some Gemini robots were able to get actual work done in Mercedes-Benz factories, and the team is preparing for a day when robots operate alongside humans with an open source safety benchmark. DeepMind's physical AI platform has several computational layers between user input and robotic action. There's the vision-language model piece, which is Gemini Embodied Reasoning. Essentially, it takes your instructions and uses live video to plan how the robot can accomplish the task. The other main component is the vision-language-action (VLA) that actually generates robot actions, like moving an actuator—that's Gemini Robotics, which has been bumped to version 2.5. DeepMind says that Gemini Robotics 2.5 is much better at tasks that require a high degree of dexterity. The model was evaluated across more than 200 activities, including serving food with tongs and using a pipette, as you would see in a laboratory. Google also showed that Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid robot with Gemini Robotics 2.5 can now tie a bow with its five-fingered hands, a notable feat, because deformable objects (like ribbon) are notoriously difficult for robots to manipulate. Read full article Comments

title: Nvidia has a Jensen Huang problem—and no obvious successor
abstract: The investigation of Jensen Huang by Nvidia’s board threatens the future of one of Silicon Valley’s longest-serving executives and a key enabler of the AI boom, who has no obvious successor as leader of the world’s second-most-valuable company. Huang is fighting for survival after admitting to an extramarital affair, believed to be with an executive at a large Nvidia customer whom US officials also allege was working as a Chinese spy. The prospect that Huang could be forced out as chief executive of the US chipmaker he co-founded more than 30 years ago has alarmed investors and allies in the tech industry. Shares in Nvidia, which late last month ceded its position as the world’s most valuable to Apple amid a broader sell-off in AI stocks, had fallen more than 5 percent by midday trading on Monday. Read full article Comments

title: FDA warns GLP-1 drugs may pose risk of rare condition that causes vision loss
abstract: The Food and Drug Administration is warning that popular obesity drugs—including Ozempic, Wegovy, Zepbound, and Mounjaro—may carry a "potential increased risk" of a rare eye condition that can lead to permanent vision loss. In a drug safety communication Monday , the FDA said it will now require makers of GLP-1 receptor agonist drugs to add a warning about that risk on their drug labels. The specific eye condition it warns of is called non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy or NAION . The condition is caused by restricted blood flow to the optic nerve, which leads to swelling and cell death and ultimately damages the nerve, causing abrupt vision loss that can often be permanent. It's unknown how GLP-1 drugs may cause NAION. The condition is rare overall, occurring in somewhere between two and 10 people in 100,000 in the general population, according to the American Academy of Ophthalmology. These small numbers have made it more difficult to determine with certainty if there is a connection. Further complicating the potential link is the fact that the risk factors for developing NAION are common among patients taking GLP-1 drugs. The risk factors include diabetes, cardiovascular disease, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, metabolic syndrome, and obstructive sleep apnea. Read full article Comments

title: Polestar has a new look with its Formula 2030 concept
abstract: Perhaps only a small percentage of Ars readers will care about the Polestar 2030 concept, debuted today by the electric automaker. Spun out of Volvo—once upon a time, Polestar was a racing team—the brand has leveraged the resources of parent-automaker Geely to create electric vehicles that marry a modern minimalist style with rewarding driving dynamics . But you now can’t buy any Polestars in the US , since Geely is Chinese, and banning Chinese-owned car brands enjoys remarkable bipartisan support in Congress. The Formula 2030 is about the same length as a Polestar 2 but with a very low roofline. If anything, the two-box shape reminds me of the Saab Aero-X, one of the final concepts from the then-terminal Swedish automaker. (In many ways, Polestar has adopted Saab’s mantle.) Credit: Polestar These rear lights will show up in production Polestars. In 2008, Saab showed off the Aero-X concept. Credit: Scott Barbour/Getty Images Polestar says the concept fits into its own segment somewhere between the next Polestar 2 and the Polestar 7—it numbers its cars chronologically (mostly), not based on size—although it’s not saying if the hatchback design will go into series production. Successfully packaging rear-seat passengers and a lithium-ion battery pack is something a concept needn’t worry about, after all. Rather, it’s a styling exercise, or more than one. title: Ukraine’s fiber-optic drones get squeezed by AI data center demand
abstract: Impervious to battlefield jamming, drones physically connected to human operators by miles of fiber-optic cables have become such a common weapon of war in Ukraine that trees and fields are strewn with tangled cables thinner than fishing lines. But importing such fiber-optic material from China has become more costly as drone warfare’s needs compete with global demand from AI data centers for the same limited supply—and so Ukrainian drone makers have been adapting. Since the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022, the Ukrainians have been forced out of necessity to continually develop battlefield innovations involving first-person view (FPV) quadcopter drones and other heavier types of drones. But it was the Russian military that first deployed unjammable fiber-optic drones to repel Ukrainian forces’ cross-border incursion into the Kursk Oblast in 2024. The Ukrainians quickly followed suit in developing their own fiber-optic drones, given the drones’ capability to shrug off electronic warfare jamming that could neutralize radio-controlled drones. Russia and Ukraine have relied on Chinese suppliers for some off-the-shelf drones and a wide array of drone components, including bulk orders of fiber wound around very large spools or sometimes small finished spools ready for installation on drones. The finished spools can hold enough fiber-optic cable for drones to regularly operate at ranges of dozens of miles, and sometimes up to 62 miles (100 kilometers) in extreme cases, as reported by the independent Russian publication The Insider . Read full article Comments

title: Review: Apple's M6 MacBook Pro is good, but it's missing all the exciting stuff
abstract: I've written more than once about the weird positioning of Apple's entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro, which has always occupied an uncomfortable perch between the MacBook Air and the higher-end MacBook Pros. The best versions of this laptop, like last year's M5 refresh, come with the same basic design and external features of the higher-end MacBook Pros, just with a more modest processor and a lower ceiling for specs like RAM and storage. The lesser versions stick with older designs or other compromises, reserving Apple's most updated designs and screen technologies for the more expensive high-end models. Recall the 13-inch M1 and M2 MacBook Pros, which stuck with Apple's 2016-era MacBook Pro designs for everything , up to and including the now-abandoned Touch Bar. (If you're someone at Apple maintaining Touch Bar support into the 2030s for the sake of these two laptop models, I'd like to hear from you. Not for a story! I'd just like to know how you are.) This year's entry-level MacBook Pro mostly falls into that latter category. It does get an Apple M6 chip, and the M6 is great—rumors suggest the M6 won't get Pro, Max, or Ultra configurations, so there are some fringe benefits here that you can't get in the top-tier MacBook Pros. But it uses the same MacBook Pro design Apple has been using since 2021 . There's no touchscreen, no OLED panel, no Dynamic Island, no half-pound weight reduction, no glowing Apple logo on the lid. Read full article Comments

title: DCU shake-up: James Gunn and Peter Safran out post-merger
abstract: It's barely been two months since the controversial Paramount and Warner Bros. merger, and we've already got a shockingly unexpected ouster : Co-CEOs of the rebooted DC Universe, James Gunn and Peter Safran, are stepping down from that role despite the Hollywood rumor mill assuming that the duo would be safe. It's unclear whether the pair chose to resign or were forced out, or what will happen to their planned slate of projects beyond 2028's Superman: Man of Tomorrow , which is in post-production. Producer Jeremy Latcham—a protege of Marvel's Kevin Feige who worked with Gunn on Guardians of the Galaxy among other MCU films—will replace them. Per Gunn and Safran's joint statement : Four years ago, we set out to unite DC under one creative vision. In that time, we helped restore Superman to the heart of DC, while opening new doors and telling new stories in film and television with Peacemaker , Creature Commandos, Lanterns and Clayface. We’re immensely proud of the team that turned that ambition into something real, including the actors, crews and executives we had the opportunity to collaborate with. We’ve shared a creative history with Jeremy going back to Marvel, and we’re eager to see the perspective he brings to DC’s next chapter. We’re excited to return to what drew us to this job in the first place, which is telling the stories we love, including the next chapter of Clark and Lex’s journey in Man of Tomorrow . DCU fans are mourning the news and what it could mean for the franchise. My feelings are mixed. On the one hand, I'm on record that I’ve found the rebooted DC Universe films released thus far to be enjoyable but rather forgettable, even when the positives outweigh the negatives . (I have yet to see Clayface , which debuted to good reviews and a solid box office showing.) But HBO has done right by the DCU: I loved both seasons of Peacemaker ; Lanterns is a shining beacon of what is possible when someone is allowed to get really creative within the genre; and I'm very much looking forward to next year's Jimmy Olsen (Skylar Gisondo) series The People v. Gorilla Grodd —described as a “mockumentary crime comedy superhero series.” Read full article Comments

title: Man who lost $308,000 on sports bets sues Kalshi for offering illegal gambling
abstract: A man who lost over $308,000 making sports wagers on Kalshi is suing the prediction market for violating the state of Washington's ban on online gambling. He's trying to turn those losses into an overall victory with a lawsuit seeking a payment of over $580,000. Bellevue, Washington, resident Scott Bright's "wagering occurred at a time when it was unlawful in Washington and when the Washington Attorney General had already sued KalshiEX LLC in this Court alleging precisely that," said the gambler's lawsuit filed on September 24 in King County Superior Court. Kalshi has since filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit. While state attorneys general throughout the US are trying to shut down Kalshi for allegedly violating state gambling laws, Bright's case tests whether unsuccessful gamblers can obtain restitution from the company through individual lawsuits. title: AI 스킬 만들기 10계명: Figma→Code 자동화 실전기
abstract: 이 글에서 예로 든 스킬은 naver/design-to-ui 라는 이름의 오픈 소스로 공개되어 있습니다. 들어가며: 같은 모델, 다른 결과 AI 코딩 도구를 쓰다 보면 프롬프트에서 같은 설명을 매번 반복하게 됩니다. "이건 아이콘이니까 에셋으로 받아", "이건 그래프니까 Canvas로 그려", "색상은 하드코딩하지 말고 디자인 토큰을 써" 같은 설명이 그렇습니다. Figma 디자인을 Android 코드로 옮길 때도 마찬가지였습니다. 그래서 Claude의 스킬(Agent Skills) 기능이 공개되자마자 Figma 디자인을 Android UI로 변환하는 스킬을 만들기 시작했습니다. 목표는 프롬프트 한 번으로 완성도 높은 UI를 얻는 것이었습니다. 스킬의 효과는 생각보다 컸습니다. 2026년 3월, 같은 모델(Claude Opus 4.6)과 같은 프롬프트에 Figma Desktop MCP 서버까지 똑같이 쓰고 스킬만 바꿔 화면 하나를 조건마다 한 번씩 변환해 보았습니다. 그 결과는 다음과 같습니다. 조건 디자인 토큰(colorScheme) 참조 생성된 drawable 스킬 없음 8회 0개 범용 공식 스킬(Figma implement-design) 20회 0개 프로젝트 맞춤 스킬(figma-to-android) 39회 1개 colorScheme 참조가 많을수록 색상을 하드코딩하지 않고 디자인 토큰을 썼다는 뜻이고, drawable은 Figma의 아이콘을 실제 에셋 파일로 받아 왔는지를 보여 줍니다. 이 숫자를 어떻게 얻었는지는 계명 10 에서 다룹니다. Figma 공식 스킬이 부족해서 생긴 차이는 아닙니다. 범용 스킬은 프로젝트의 디자인 토큰과 에셋 규칙을 알 수 없고, 맞춤 스킬은 바로 그 공식 스킬 위에 프로젝트 규칙을 얹은 것입니다. 이 방식은 계명 2 에서 자세히 다룹니다. Figma 원본과 세 조건으로 변환한 날씨 화면(오토앱)을 나란히 놓으면 다음과 같습니다. 지역과 날씨 데이터는 Figma 시안의 예시 값이거나 캡처 시점의 실제 값이라 서로 다릅니다. Figma 원본 ① 스킬 없음 ② 범용 공식 스킬 ③ 프로젝트 맞춤 스킬 그림 1 Figma 원본(위)과 세 조건으로 변환한 날씨 화면(아래) 모델은 같았는데 결과물의 디테일은 확연히 달랐습니다. 예를 들어 '서울시 명동' 옆 위치 아이콘은 맞춤 스킬에서만 제대로 나왔고, 시간별 기온 그래프도 맞춤 스킬에서만 그려졌습니다. 다만 이 스킬을 틈틈이 만드는 데 3개월쯤 걸렸습니다. 이 글에서는 3개월 동안 알게 된 원칙 10가지를 정리했습니다. 처음부터 알았다면 그 시간을 크게 줄일 수 있었을 것입니다. 사내 Engineering Day에서 발표한 내용을 글로 옮기면서 발표에서 다 하지 못한 사례를 더했습니다. 스킬은 무엇이고 프롬프트와 무엇이 다른가 스킬은 특정 작업을 어떻게 해야 하는지 적어 둔 폴더입니다. 폴더에는 SKILL.md 파일이 하나 있고, 필요하면 참고 문서( references/ )와 스크립트( scripts/ )를 함께 넣습니다. Claude는 평소에는 스킬의 이름과 설명만 알고 있다가, 요청이 그 설명과 맞으면 SKILL.md 본문을 읽어 들여 그 지침에 따라 작업합니다. 프롬프트와의 차이는 세 가지입니다. 반복 설명이 사라집니다. 매번 프롬프트에 붙여 넣던 에셋 규칙과 변환 절차를 스킬에 한 번만 적어 두면 됩니다. 스크립트를 함께 넣을 수 있습니다. 말로 설명하기 어렵고 결과가 늘 같아야 하는 작업(예: SVG를 VectorDrawable로 변환)은 스크립트로 만들어 두고 Claude가 실행하게 합니다. 팀이 같이 키울 수 있습니다. 파일이라 버전 관리가 되고, 플러그인으로 묶어 배포할 수 있습니다. 이 글의 예시는 Claude Code 기준이지만, 같은 스킬 형식(Agent Skills)을 지원하는 다른 에이전트 도구에도 대부분 적용됩니다. 이 글에 자주 나오는 용어를 먼저 정리합니다. 용어 뜻 MCP(Model Context Protocol) AI 도구가 외부 프로그램(이 글에서는 Figma)과 데이터를 주고받는 표준 방식 frontmatter SKILL.md 맨 위에 스킬의 이름과 설명 등을 적는 메타데이터 영역 디자인 토큰 색상, 글자 크기처럼 디자인 시스템이 이름을 붙여 관리하는 값. Compose의 colorScheme.primary 처럼 colorScheme 에 모아 둔 색상 값이 그 예다. 토큰(LLM) AI 모델이 글을 처리하는 단위. 디자인 토큰과는 다르며, 스킬이 길수록 많이 쓴다. drawable, VectorDrawable Android 앱의 이미지 리소스와 그 벡터 형식 Canvas 코드로 직접 도형을 그리는 Android API gotcha Claude가 반복해서 실수하는 지점과 그 해결책을 적은 기록 에셋 A/B/C Figma의 그래픽 요소를 처리 방식에 따라 정적 에셋(A), 동적 비주얼(B), 기존 에셋(C)으로 나눈 것. 자세한 기준은 계명 6 에서 다룬다. 스킬 만들기 10계명 10계명은 사전 점검(1∼2), 본문 설계(3∼7), 검증과 개선(8∼10) 세 단계로 나뉩니다. 각 계명에는 스스로 던져 볼 핵심 질문과 figma-to-android 스킬을 만들며 겪은 실제 사례를 덧붙였습니다. 사전 점검 스킬을 만들기 전에 확인할 것들입니다. 스킬에 무엇을 담을지 직접 해 보며 찾고, 쓸 만한 스킬이 이미 있는지 살펴봅니다. 계명 1. 스킬부터 만들지 마라 — 먼저 직접 해 봐라 핵심 질문: 스킬 없이 해 보면서 무엇을 반복해서 설명했나? /skill-creator 에 원하는 스킬을 설명하면 형식에 맞는 스킬을 금방 만들어 줍니다. 하지만 그보다 먼저 스킬 없이 프롬프트만으로 작업을 해 봐야 합니다. 그러면서 세 가지를 관찰합니다. 매번 반복해서 설명하는 정보 Claude가 놓치는 것 사람이 손으로 고쳐 주는 패턴 이 세 가지가 스킬에 들어갈 내용입니다. Anthropic에서 Claude Code를 만드는 Thariq Shihipar도 Lessons from building Claude Code: How we use skills 에서 같은 이야기를 합니다. 뻔한 내용은 빼고 Claude의 기본 행동을 바꾸는 정보에 집중하라고 하면서, Anthropic의 좋은 스킬도 대부분 몇 줄짜리 지시와 gotcha 하나로 시작했다고 말합니다. 저는 반대로 했습니다. 처음부터 목표(Figma → Compose)와 필요할 것 같은 자료(Figma와 Compose의 매핑 정보)를 한꺼번에 주고 스킬을 만들어 달라고 했습니다. 그 결과 700줄이 넘는 스킬에서 출발했고, Claude는 긴 지시를 제대로 따르지 못했습니다. 이것이 3개월 동안 가장 큰 병목이었습니다. 그림 2 Compose와 XML을 함께 지원하도록 스킬을 다시 만들 때 쓴 프롬프트 다시 직접 날씨 화면을 변환해 보니 매번 "colorScheme을 써라", "SVG를 VectorDrawable로 변환해라", "기존 drawable이 있는지 확인해라"를 반복하고 있었습니다. 이 세 문장이 스킬의 핵심이 됐습니다. 단, 이미 절차를 잘 아는 워크플로를 스킬로 옮길 때는 "만들어 줘"로 시작해도 괜찮습니다. 계명 2. 기존 스킬 위에 쌓아라 — 바퀴를 재발명하지 마라 핵심 질문: 비슷한 공식 스킬이나 커뮤니티 스킬은 없나? 만들기 전에 비슷한 스킬이 이미 있는지부터 찾아봅니다. 검증된 구조 위에 도메인 특화 부분만 얹는 편이 훨씬 빠르고 안정적입니다. anthropics/skills : Anthropic 공식 스킬 저장소 figma/mcp-server-guide : Figma 공식 스킬과 MCP 가이드 사내 스킬 저장소 Figma가 공식 스킬 implement-design을 공개한 뒤에는 그 워크플로를 뼈대로 가져왔습니다. 이 스킬은 2026년 3월 figma-implement-design으로 이름이 바뀌었고 5월에 저장소에서 삭제됐지만, 워크플로를 figma-to-android 안에 옮겨 두었기 때문에 영향은 없었습니다. figma-to-android의 7단계는 Step 1(Node ID 추출), Step 2(디자인 컨텍스트), Step 3(스크린숏), Step 4(에셋 분

title: 우리 팀만의 스펙 주도 개발 정착기
abstract: 네이버 사내 기술 교류 행사인 NAVER Engineering Day 10th 에서 발표되었던 세션을 공개합니다. ​ 우리 팀만의 스펙 주도 개발 정착기 NAVER D2 | 우리 팀만의 스펙 주도 개발 정착기 naver.me ​ 발표 내용 스펙 주도 개발(SDD)을 팀 내 개발 정책으로 채택한 배경과 시행착오에 대해 소개합니다. ​ 발표 대상 스펙 주도 개발 도입을 고민중인 개발자 ​ 목차 배경 - SDD를 도입하게 된 이유 우리 팀이 채택한 SDD의 구조 팀 SDD 정책을 세우며 마주친 고민 일곱갈래 다음 고민과 남은 숙제 ​ ​ ◎ NAVER Engineering Day란? ​ NAVER에서는 사내 개발 경험과 기술 트렌드를 교류를 할 수 있는 프로그램이 많이 있습니다. 그중 이제는 매회 평균 100개 이상의 발표가 이루어지는 NAVER Engineering Day를 빼놓을 수 없는데요. 2016년부터 시작된 ENGINEERING DAY는 실무에서의 기술 개발 경험과 새로운 기술과 플랫폼 도입 시 유용하게 활용될 수 있는 팁 등을 공유하며 서로 배우고 성장하는 네이버의 대표적인 사내 개발자 행사입니다.( 관련 포스팅 보기 ) 올해 진행된 NAVER Engineering Day의 일부 세션을 공개합니다. ​ [동영상 제공 채널 안내] 네이버 TV 서비스 종료로 인해 기존 네이버 TV 채널을 클립( @devrel_d2 )으로 이동하였습니다. 앞으로도 많은 관심과 팔로우 부탁드리겠습니다.

title: 실행은 격리하고, 세션은 이어간다: 망분리 환경의 Agent Platform 설계기
abstract: 초기 Agent Platform의 대화 화면. 사용자가 Agent를 선택하고 업무를 요청합니다. “지난달과 같은 기준으로 이번 달 데이터도 비교해줘.” 데이터를 분석하다 보면 자주 받는 요청입니다. 지난번에 쓴 쿼리를 찾아 기간을 바꾸고, 실행 결과를 비교해야 하죠. 빠진 데이터는 없는지, 집계 기준은 그대로인지도 확인해야 합니다. AI Platform 팀은 사람이 매번 반복하던 이 과정을 에이전트가 처리하도록 만들고 싶었습니다. 토스는 「 전자금융감독규정 」의 망분리 요건에 따라 금융 업무를 처리하는 내부망과 인터넷 업무 환경을 분리해 운영하고 있습니다. 자동화하려던 분석에 필요한 데이터도 내부망에 있었고, 외부로 옮길 수 없었습니다. 사람이 내부 도구로 하던 조회와 가공을 대신하려면, 에이전트가 내부망에서 코드를 실행하고 데이터를 분석할 수 있어야 했습니다. 그렇다고 에이전트에게 내부망의 모든 파일과 시스템을 열어줄 수는 없었습니다. 모델이 만든 코드가 작업과 관계없는 데이터를 읽거나 파일을 잘못 수정할 수도 있기 때문입니다. 프롬프트로 주의를 주는 것만으로는 이런 실수를 막기 어려웠습니다. 그래서 에이전트의 코드를 샌드박스 안에서 실행하고, 작업에 필요한 파일과 시스템에만 접근하도록 제한했습니다. 이전에 하던 작업을 이어가는 것도 중요했습니다. “지난달과 같은 기준으로 비교해줘”라는 요청을 처리하려면, 지난번에 사용한 코드와 집계 기준을 알아야 하니까요. 매번 새 환경에서 시작한다면 사용자는 코드를 다시 준비하고 분석 기준도 다시 설명해야 합니다. 사용자가 같은 내용을 매번 준비하지 않아도 되도록, 작업 파일과 대화 상태를 보관하기로 했습니다. 이 글에서는 이 두 가지 요구를 바탕으로 Agent Platform을 설계한 과정을 소개합니다. 샌드박스에서 파일과 네트워크 접근을 어떻게 제한했는지 실행 환경이 바뀌어도 작업을 계속할 수 있도록 파일과 대화 상태를 어떻게 관리했는지 모델이 만든 코드는 어디에서 실행할까 플랫폼 관리 기능은 Workspace 밖에 두고, 모델이 만든 코드와 명령은 Workspace 안의 제한된 환경에서 실행합니다. *구조도에 나오는 GenAI Gateway와 MCP Gateway의 역할이 궁금하다면 이전 글 을 참고해 주세요. 모델은 어떤 코드를 실행할지 결정할 수 있지만, 스스로 프로세스를 띄우거나 파일을 고치지는 않습니다. 모델의 응답에 따라 도구를 실행하고, 그 결과를 다시 모델에 전달하는 프로그램이 필요하죠. 이 과정을 반복하는 프로그램을 하네스(harness) 라고 부릅니다. 분석 코드에 오류가 나면 그 내용을 모델에 전달하고, 수정한 코드를 다시 실행하는 것도 하네스가 맡습니다. 모델과 도구를 반복해서 호출하는 일은 기존 하네스에 맡겼습니다. 플랫폼은 요청자가 누구인지 확인하고, 작업에 필요한 실행 환경과 접근 권한을 준비합니다. 이렇게 역할을 나누면 하네스를 교체하더라도 사용자 관리나 저장소 연결을 다시 구현할 필요가 없습니다. 한 사용자가 여러 에이전트와 대화할 수 있으므로, 실행할 때는 누구의 작업 공간인지, 어떤 에이전트의 대화인지 구분해야 합니다. Workspace : 사용자마다 제공하는 개인 작업 공간 Agent : 업무 지침과 사용할 도구를 설정한 에이전트 Session : 각 Agent와 나누는 개별 대화 예를 들어 한 Workspace 안에 데이터 분석 Agent와 문서 작성 Agent를 두고, 분석 Agent와 월별로 다른 대화를 나눌 수 있습니다. Agent나 대화마다 실행 환경을 만들면 환경 준비와 저장소 연결도 반복해야 합니다. 이 반복을 줄이기 위해 사용자마다 Kubernetes의 실행 단위인 Pod를 만들고, Workspace의 실행 환경으로 재사용하기로 했습니다. 하나의 Pod를 함께 쓰더라도 Agent마다 접근할 수 있는 파일과 시스템은 제한해야 합니다. Agent의 지침과 도구 설정에 따라 실제 작업을 수행하는 것은 하네스입니다. 그래서 하네스를 격리하고, 그 안에서 실행한 도구와 코드에도 같은 접근 제한이 적용되도록 했습니다. Workspace의 실행 환경은 오픈소스 OpenSandbox 로 관리합니다. OpenSandbox가 Kubernetes에 Workspace별 Pod를 만들고 종료하는 일을 맡습니다. Runtime은 Pod 안에서 하네스를 바로 실행하지 않습니다. 먼저 bubblewrap으로 접근할 폴더와 통신 경로를 제한한 환경을 만들고, 그 안에서 하네스와 도구를 실행합니다. 사용자가 화면에서 분석을 요청하면 다음 순서로 실행을 준비합니다. Server 가 사용자와 리소스 접근 권한을 확인 Runner 가 해당 Workspace의 실행 환경을 준비하고 Runtime에 실행 설정을 전달 Runtime 이 설정에 맞춰 하네스를 격리하고 실행 실행 준비가 끝나면 하네스가 모델과 도구를 호출하며 작업을 진행합니다. 사용자는 화면에서 응답과 실행 결과를 확인할 수 있습니다. Server와 Runner는 Workspace Pod 밖에서 동작합니다. 하네스에는 업무에 필요한 입력과 도구를 제공하지만, 플랫폼 DB의 인증정보는 넘기지 않습니다. 분석 코드를 실행하는 데 다른 사용자의 설정이나 플랫폼 관리 기능에 접근할 권한까지 필요한 것은 아니니까요. 같은 Pod 안에서 Agent의 접근 범위를 나누기 Runtime은 Agent마다 허용한 폴더를 연결하고, 격리된 환경의 통신을 HTTP 프록시로 연결합니다. 같은 Workspace를 사용해도 각 Agent가 접근할 수 있는 파일은 다릅니다. 분석 Agent는 분석에 필요한 참고 문서를 읽을 수 있어야 합니다. 그렇다고 문서 작성 Agent의 작업 파일까지 마음대로 바꿀 수 있어서는 안 되겠죠. 화면에서 도구 목록을 숨기거나 파일 읽기 도구에서만 권한을 확인하는 것으로는 부족했습니다. 하네스가 셸 명령이나 직접 작성한 프로그램으로 같은 파일을 열 수도 있기 때문입니다. 그래서 도구의 종류와 관계없이, 코드를 실행하는 프로세스 자체의 접근 범위를 제한 하기로 했습니다. Runtime은 bubblewrap 을 사용해 하네스마다 별도의 Linux namespace를 구성합니다. namespace는 프로세스마다 파일시스템의 마운트 구성, 프로세스 목록, 네트워크 등을 격리할 수 있는 Linux 기능입니다. Agent마다 별도 VM을 두면 게스트 커널까지 나눌 수 있습니다. 다만 VM별로 이미지와 작업 볼륨을 준비하고, 생성과 종료를 플랫폼의 실행 흐름에 연결해야 합니다. 저희가 필요로 한 것은 Workspace의 실행 환경을 재사용하면서, 그 안에서 하네스마다 파일과 통신 접근 범위를 다르게 설정하는 것이었습니다. 이를 위해 기존 Kubernetes와 OpenSandbox 구성 안에서 bubblewrap으로 하네스를 격리하는 방식을 선택했습니다. 실행 환경의 생성과 종료는 Workspace 단위로 관리하고, 하네스를 실행할 때 허용한 폴더와 통신 경로만 연결했습니다. Agent마다 별도의 게스트 운영체제를 준비하고 관리하지 않아도 필요한 접근 제한을 적용할 수 있었습니다. 다만 호스트 커널을 공유하므로 VM과 같은 커널 격리를 제공하지는 않습니다. 두 방식의 차이는 다음과 같습니다. 방식 장점 플랫폼에서 준비하고 관리할 것 Agent마다 별도 VM 사용 Agent마다 게스트 커널을 따로 사용하는 격리 환경을 구성할 수 있음 VM 생성과 종료, 이미지 준비, 작업 볼륨 연결을 플랫폼 실행 흐름과 연동 Workspace Pod 안에서 namespace 사용 기존 Workspace 안에서 하네스마다 파일과 네트워크 접근 범위를 설정할 수 있음 기존 Kubernetes/OpenSandbox 구성을 활용하면서, 하네스별 파일/네트워크/실행 권한을 설정하고 격리 동작을 검증 같은 Pod 안에서 실행하더라도, 각 하네스에 필요한 파일과 통신 경로만 제공해야 합니다. 이를 위해 Runtime은 하네스를 실행할 때 다음 세 가지를 제한합니다. 1️⃣ 접근할 수 있는 파일 실행에 필요한 기본 파일 외에는 Agent의 작업 폴더, 사용자가 추가로 허용한 폴더, 현재 세션의 상태가 저장된 경로만 마운트합니다. 마운트는 실제 디렉터리를

title: TASTE, 토스의 추천 파운데이션 플랫폼
abstract: 금융 상품에 관심이 있는 사람을 찾는 모델, 푸시를 클릭할 사람을 찾는 모델, 좋아할 미니앱을 추천하는 모델. 풀어야 할 문제는 다르지만, 이해해야 하는 대상은 모두 같은 토스의 사용자입니다. 토스에 쌓이는 방대하고 서로 다른 데이터를 충분히 학습하여 배운 내용을 여러 추천 문제에 활용할 수는 없을까요? TASTE(Toss Automated Standard Targeting Engine) 는 이 질문에서 시작했습니다. 사용자의 다양한 행동을 함께 예측하고, 그 과정에서 배운 ‘사용자 표현’을 다른 서비스 모델에 전달하고자 했습니다. 여러 서비스의 온오프라인 실험에서 이 표현이 예측에 도움이 된다는 것까지 확인했습니다. 이 글에서는 여러 행동을 함께 학습하고, 그 과정에서 얻은 사용자 표현을 다른 추천 모델에 전달하며, 이를 다시 개선하는 과정 을 소개합니다. 한 번 배운 사용자 정보를 여러 추천 문제에 활용하는 것, 이것이 저희가 생각하는 추천 파운데이션 모델의 출발점입니다. 같은 사용자를 모델마다 다시 배우고 있었습니다 토스에는 금융중개, 광고, 쇼핑, 결제, Apps in Toss 등 여러 서비스가 있습니다. 서비스가 늘어날수록 클릭, 구매, 전환 등을 예측하는 모델도 늘어납니다. 모델마다 목표는 달라도 사용하는 사용자 정보는 겹치는 부분이 많습니다. 나이와 같은 속성, 앱에서 이용한 기능, 소비 이력 등이 대표적입니다. 각 모델은 이 정보를 자신의 예측에 필요한 형태로 가공하고 학습합니다. 같은 정보를 모델마다 따로 준비하고 학습하면서 중복 작업이 생겼습니다. 데이터를 충분히 활용하는 일도 쉽지 않았습니다. 토스는 월간 활성 사용자(MAU)가 2천만 명을 넘어, 주요 서버 로그만 해도 하루에 수십억 건 이상 쌓입니다. 사용자 한 명을 이해하기 위해 살펴봐야 할 정보도 방대합니다. 데이터의 성격도 제각각입니다. 마이데이터는 수십 개의 API를 통해 들어오며, 데이터마다 수집 시점과 정보를 확보할 수 있는 사용자 범위가 다릅니다. 외부 앱 이용 정보를 담은 MMP 데이터는 이벤트가 지나치게 많거나, 반대로 너무 적기도 합니다. 서버 로그와 마이데이터, MMP 데이터는 활용하고 분석할 수 있는 동의 조건도 모두 다릅니다. 결국 각 모델은 예측 문제를 풀기에 앞서, 이 방대하고 서로 다른 데이터를 어떻게 모으고 학습할지부터 해결해야 했습니다. 서비스별 예측 모델은 응답 시간 등 서비스가 요구하는 수준(SLA)을 맞춰야 해서 상대적으로 크기가 작습니다. 이런 제약 아래에서 개별 모델이 방대한 정보를 충분히 학습하기는 쉽지 않습니다. 그래서 서비스 중인 모델들이 예측에 도움이 되는 사용자 정보를 놓치고 있을 수 있다는 가설을 세웠습니다. 모델을 합치는 것만으로는 성능이 좋아지지 않았습니다 “ 여러 모델에 필요한 사용자 표현을 한 번에 학습하고, 그 결과를 여러 목적에 활용할 수 있을까? ” 먼저 주요 앱이벤트를 동시에 예측하는 멀티태스크 학습을 시도했습니다. 사용자 정보를 예측에 필요한 표현으로 바꾸는 인코더(Encoder)를 공유하고, 그 뒤에 결제나 특정 서비스 이용 등 과제별 예측을 담당하는 헤드(Head)를 붙이는 방식입니다. 같은 정보를 받아도 과제마다 필요한 부분은 다릅니다. 과제별로 필요한 정보를 다르게 조합할 수 있도록, 처음에는 MMoE(Multi-gate Mixture-of-Experts) 구조를 시도했습니다. 빠르게 가능성을 살펴보기 위해 초기에는 학습 사용자를 100만 명으로 줄였습니다. 사용자 수를 줄인 영향을 살펴볼 수 있도록, 기존 모델에 사용하던 LightGBM도 100만 명 규모로 학습했습니다. 같은 사용자 수로 학습한 두 모델을 비교했을 때, MMoE의 성능(AUROC)은 과제별로 따로 학습한 LightGBM보다 낮았습니다. 이 결과만으로는 여러 과제를 함께 학습하는 방식의 이점을 확인하기 어려웠습니다. 학습 데이터와 모델을 확장하자 성능이 올랐습니다 하지만 저희는 다른 가설을 세웠습니다. “ 한 모델이 여러 행동을 동시에 예측하려면, 각 행동을 따로 학습할 때보다 더 많은 데이터가 필요한 것 아닐까? ” 공동학습 자체의 한계로 결론짓기 전에, 더 많은 사용자와 더 풍부한 행동 정보를 학습해보기로 했습니다. 우선 학습 대상을 100만 명에서 학습에 사용할 수 있는 전체 사용자로 넓혔습니다. 사용자 요약 정보도 기존 1,000여 개에서 2,000개 이상으로 늘렸습니다. 요약 정보에 담기지 않은 행동의 흐름도 배울 수 있도록, 최근 앱이벤트 시퀀스를 Causal Transformer로 읽고 압축했습니다. 늘어난 입력에 맞춰 모델 구조도 개선했습니다. 요약 정보를 처리하는 인코더에는 DCN-V2를, 과제별 예측을 담당하는 부분에는 PLE(Progressive Layered Extraction)를 사용했습니다. 학습 사용자 규모와 입력 피처, 모델 구조를 확대한 뒤에는 기존 모델의 성능을 넘어설 수 있었습니다. 공통 앱이벤트 예측에서 Macro Recall@5k의 상대 개선율은 약 35.1%입니다. 초기의 낮은 성능을 공동학습의 한계로 받아들이지 않고 가설을 세워 실험한 결과입니다. 사용자 요약 정보를 2,000개 이상 사용하면서 새로운 의문도 생겼습니다. 요약 정보가 충분하다면 시퀀스 모듈은 없어도 되지 않을까요? 이를 확인하기 위해 시퀀스 모듈을 제거한 별도 실험을 진행했고, Macro Recall@5k가 상대적으로 7.6% 낮아지는 것을 확인했습니다. 많은 요약 정보를 사용하더라도, 시퀀스를 직접 학습하면 예측에 도움이 된다는 정보를 추가로 얻었습니다. 소비까지 함께 배우며 목적에 맞는 구조를 찾았습니다 앱이벤트 공동학습의 성과를 바탕으로, 주요 소비 이벤트까지 학습 범위를 넓혔습니다. 앱이벤트 시퀀스가 요약 정보를 보완했던 것처럼, 소비도 이력을 직접 학습하면 도움이 될 것이라고 생각했습니다. 그래서 미래 소비를 예측하는 과제와 함께, 브랜드·카테고리 등의 소비 시퀀스를 읽는 인코더를 추가했습니다. 하지만 한 모델에서 모두 학습하자 과제별 성과가 달라졌습니다. 소비 예측은 기존 개별 모델보다 좋아졌지만, 앱이벤트의 Macro Recall@5k는 앱이벤트만 한 번에 학습했을 때보다 낮아졌습니다. 앱이벤트와 소비는 행동의 성격도, 정답 데이터가 들어오는 시점도 크게 달랐습니다. 두 목적을 예측하는 데 필요한 표현과 학습 방식도 다를 수 있었습니다. 그래서 각 목적에 맞는 표현을 따로 학습하면 성능을 개선할 수 있을 것 이라는 가설을 세웠습니다. 입력 정보는 함께 활용하되, 앱이벤트와 소비를 예측하는 모델은 인코더부터 따로 학습했습니다. 두 모델 모두 앱이벤트 이력, 소비 이력, 사용자 요약 정보를 받으며, 각 모델 안에서는 여전히 여러 앱이벤트 또는 소비 과제를 함께 학습합니다. 모델별로 구조를 탐색하고 최적화해, 각 목적에 맞는 학습 방식을 찾았습니다. 목적을 나누고 각 모델의 구조와 학습 방법을 개선한 결과, 앱이벤트의 Macro Recall@5k는 단일 모델 TASTE보다 8.7% 높아졌습니다. 소비 예측은 같은 지표에서 기존 모델 대비 브랜드 33.9%, 중분류 111%, 소분류 65.8% 개선됐습니다. 여러 과제를 함께 학습하는 이점을 살리면서도, 목적에 맞게 모델을 나누고 최적화해 각 서비스에 필요한 성능을 확보할 수 있었습니다. 학습한 모델을 실제 운영에 연결했습니다 TASTE가 제공하는 결과물은 크게 두 가지입니다. 하나는 모델이 직접 계산한 행동별 예측 확률이고, 다른 하나는 학습한 사용자 정보를 담은 임베딩입니다. 먼저 예측 확률을 실제 운영에 활용한 사례를 소개하겠습니다. 우선 여러 과제를 함께 학습하면서 개별 모델마다 반복하던 데이터 준비·학습·추론 작업을 통합하고, 중복되는 인프라 사용과 운영 부담을 줄였습니다. 이렇게 생성한 확률값은 목표 행동을 할 가능성이 높은 사용자를 찾는 데 활용했습니다. 토스에서 IM(Intelligence Manager)은 홈 상단 배너를 노출하고 푸시, SMS·LMS, 브랜드톡을 발송하는 통합 메시지 발송 허브입니다. 캠페인 담당자가 많은 시간을 쓰는 일 중 하나는 ‘누구에게 보낼까’를 정하는 것이었습니다. 같은 푸시라도 목표에 따라 어떤 행동 이

title: Guiding Data Allocation for Robust Subpopulation Generalization
abstract: Machine learning models often achieve high average accuracy in the training data while performing poorly on test data due to subpopulation shift. A common data-centric solution is to enforce balanced subgroup proportions, but full balance can be costly, infeasible, and not always necessary. In this work, we study whether balanced training data is the unique optimal configuration for robust subpopulation generalization. We extend a Gaussian feature-model framework to theoretically characterize the performance landscape across general training subgroup distributions. We show that multiple configurations, including substantially imbalanced ones, can perform comparably to the balanced one. We further derive gradient-based directions for adjusting subgroup proportions to improve adjusted accuracy and worst-group accuracy more efficiently. These findings suggest that strategically allocating data offers a more flexible and principled path to robust performance than simple balancing. The code is available at https://github.com/zhaoyingpan/subpop-data-allocation.

title: Vendi Anomaly Scores for Efficient and Accurate Anomaly Detection
abstract: Anomaly detection (AD) is a critical for trustworthy machine learning and scientific discovery. Existing methods typically define anomalies through local density, isolation heuristics, or distance from a fitted distribution, making them sensitive to neighborhood scale, partitioning choices, or restrictive distributional assumptions. In this work, we introduce a new paradigm by formulating anomaly detection from a diversity perspective. We propose the $\textit{Vendi Anomaly Score}$ (VAS), which detects anomalies by quantifying how much a sample changes the diversity of the dataset, as measured by the Vendi score, when removed. VAS captures both local redundancy and global data structure without relying on density estimation or partitioning heuristics. Moreover, VAS requires no hyperparameter tuning, instead adapting automatically to the spectral structure of the data. VAS is non-parametric and scales linearly with dataset size. Across 148 benchmark embedding datasets derived from 10 source datasets and 4 embedding architectures, VAS achieves state-of-the-art AD performance. We further validate VAS on large-scale ImageNet experiments, where it remains robust as both contamination rate and dataset scale increase.

title: Where Does Alignment Emerge and What Does It Mean? A Closer Look at the Platonic Representation Hypothesis
abstract: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) suggests that neural networks are converging toward similar representation spaces. As language models become more capable, their representations are aligning with those of vision models. However, recent work has questioned whether this trend continues to hold for newer language models. Moreover, it has been shown that representation similarity metrics can be confounded by model depth and width, requiring appropriate baselines for interpretation. In this work, we first investigate where alignment emerges between unimodal models across model layers and representation dimensions. Next, we find that the PRH capability-alignment trend persists for newer models as long as the captions are sufficiently clean and informative. Finally, we contextualize cross-modal alignment, introducing unimodal and multimodal baselines on various datasets. Our results show that the cross-modal representational alignment of unimodal models can surpass that of explicitly aligned vision-language models, but remains substantially behind the alignment observed for models of the same modality. Code is available at https://github.com/ExplainableML/prh-closer-look.

title: What kills $v$-prediction? A Patch-wise PCA Perspective on Pixel-Space Flow Matching
abstract: Latent Diffusion Models dominate generative modeling but face two-stage training complexity and the inherent reconstruction limits of pre-trained autoencoders. Pixel-space Flow Matching offers a simplified end-to-end alternative yet often encounters training difficulties when using the standard $v$-prediction objective. Recent research attributes this difficulty to the off-manifold nature of noised targets, motivating a shift toward $x$-prediction. In this paper, we investigate this explanation through patch-wise Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and identify a bandwidth bottleneck. The velocity in minor components is largely determined by the raw noisy input, requiring deep backbones to preserve information that competes with principal-component modeling. Through controlled experiments and representation analysis, we further examine why $x$-prediction remains effective: its parameterization provides a raw-input bypass, while its learned input representation can spontaneously concentrate on principal directions. Under low-rank observations, our analysis of the induced flow characterizes $x$-prediction as an implicit conditional-mean decoder, reconstructing discarded components from the retained information. These observations motivate the Raw-injected Transformer (RiT), which combines a lightweight raw-conditioned decoder with an output-side shortcut to separate semantic modeling from raw-state propagation. Our method restores effective $v$-prediction and achieves competitive performance on ImageNet $256\times256$, providing a perspective on the interaction between prediction objectives and architectural bandwidth.

title: MaxIM: Maximally Informative Incremental Summarization via Reinforcement Learning
abstract: AI systems must often maintain bounded memory of unbounded interaction histories. However, optimizing the memory representation, and its updates, for downstream task utility is difficult for standard reinforcement learning (RL) due to severe credit assignment bottlenecks induced by sparse, delayed rewards. We introduce MaxIM (Maximally Informative Incremental Memory), a framework that formulates incremental summarization as a capacity-constrained, information-theoretic reward-shaping problem. Grounded in value suboptimality bounds, we show that bounding sequential information loss motivates maximizing the predictive log-likelihood of future, task-relevant targets, a variational lower bound on predictive sufficiency. We introduce a recursive consistency condition to ensure summaries are grounded by maximizing mutual information (MI) with the observed history. We mitigate credit assignment issues with a parameterized asymmetric critic that computes step-wise variational MI bounds for dense reward shaping. Empirical evaluation on long-horizon scientific reading and multi-turn dialogue benchmarks shows that MaxIM outperforms RL, supervised fine-tuning, and prompt-focused baselines on factual grounding, comprehensive autorater metrics, and downstream task utility across strict token budgets and extended horizons, without the need for expensive human preference labels.

title: 2D Gum-Net: Unsupervised Dense Elastic Image Registration via Symmetric Correlation and Spectral Pooling
abstract: Dense non-rigid registration, the recovery of a pixel-wise deformation field that warps one image into geometric agreement with another, is fundamental across medical imaging, structural biology, and correspondence estimation, yet learning-based approaches face a severe bottleneck: ground-truth deformation fields are notoriously difficult to obtain for real data. We present 2D Gum-Net, an end-to-end architecture that predicts dense elastic deformation fields fully unsupervised. We transfer the Geometric Unsupervised Matching Network (Gum-Net), originally developed for 3D subtomogram alignment in cryo-electron tomography, to 2D elastic registration: all three modules are redesigned in 2D, and the rigid transformation head is replaced by a Dense Spatial Transformer that regresses a sparse control-point grid, lifted to a full-resolution field $Φ$ by bicubic interpolation. Downsampling uses DCT spectral pooling, implemented as frozen-basis matrix multiplications ($\approx 50\times$ GPU speedup), preserving the fine, quasi-periodic structure that max and average pooling destroy. We evaluate on contact-based fingerprints, a challenging testbed for this task: locally self-similar ridge patterns make correspondence maximally ambiguous, skin pressed against a sensor generates authentic large-displacement elastic distortion, and minutiae act as precise landmarks through which an independent matcher externally verifies the topological correctness of predicted fields.
